stems.explanation: When mAs is unchanged. Lower kVp reduces photon output and penetration, so receptor exposure falls.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increase scatter to patient.
stems.explanation: Decreasing kVp generally reduces Compton scatter production; increasing kVp tends to increase scatter fraction.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increase scatter to receptors.
stems.explanation: Decreasing kVp generally reduces Compton scatter production; increasing kVp tends to increase scatter fraction.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increase contrast.
stems.explanation: For lowering kVp. Reduced penetration and a greater photoelectric contribution increase subject contrast, although receptor exposure and noise also change.

stems.label: A
stems.text: PET+Ct are done sequentially.
stems.explanation: PET/CT acquires CT and PET sequentially during the same examination, then fuses the datasets.

title: Regarding if use high resolution CT technique will increase resolution to 15 lp/mm

stems.label: A
stems.text: if use high resolution Ct technique will increase resolution to 15 lp/mm.
stems.explanation: Routine CT spatial resolution is far below 15 line pairs per millimetre; that value is associated with mammographic resolution.

title: Regarding diameter of contrast used in u/s is equal to diameter of probe thickness

stems.label: A
stems.text: diameter of contrast used in U/S is equal to diameter of probe thickness.
stems.explanation: Contrast microbubbles are only a few micrometres in diameter, much smaller than the ultrasound wavelength and unrelated to probe thickness.

title: Regarding ESD means measure exposure in an area of only 100cm2

stems.label: A
stems.text: ESD means measure exposure in an area of only 100cm2.
stems.explanation: ESD is entrance surface dose at the skin; dose-area product is the quantity involving irradiated area.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Intensity.
stems.explanation: If saying filtration increases intensity: filtration removes photons, although it increases mean beam energy.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Amount of scatter reaching film.
stems.explanation: Filtration removes low-energy photons, reducing skin dose and increasing beam quality/HVL.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Dose.
stems.explanation: If saying filtration increases patient dose: added filtration generally lowers entrance skin dose.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Surface area of filament increases amount of x-rays produced.
stems.explanation: Filament/focal spot size affects heat loading and focal spot geometry; tube current/mA primarily controls the number of X-rays produced.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Contains xenon gas.
stems.explanation: An X-ray tube contains a vacuum, not xenon gas.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Heat is regulated by conduction.
stems.explanation: Most anode heat is dissipated by radiation to the tube housing and then conduction/convection through cooling systems, not simply by conduction within the vacuum.

stems.label: A
stems.text: High contrast.
stems.explanation: High kV reduces subject contrast because the beam is more penetrating and Compton scatter dominates.

stems.label: B
stems.text: High beam intensity.
stems.explanation: Tube output increases strongly with kVp, approximately proportional to kVp squared.

title: Regarding scatter is reduced by compression

stems.label: A
stems.text: Scatter is reduced by compression.
stems.explanation: Mammography uses low-energy spectra, compression and high spatial resolution while minimising glandular dose.

title: Regarding CR, size of phosphor affects sensitivity

stems.label: A
stems.text: Regarding CR, size of phosphor affects sensitivity.
stems.explanation: Phosphor layer thickness and crystal properties affect x ray absorption, sensitivity and spatial resolution.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Typical matrix size is 256x256.
stems.explanation: A conventional CT image matrix is typically 512 x 512, although other matrices can be selected.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing matrix size from 512x512 to 1024x1024 doubles the amount of storage required.
stems.explanation: Quadruples. False if it says doubles: 512 x 512 to 1024 x 1024 quadruples the pixel count and storage.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Tissue in the centre may have a lower HU than actual value.
stems.explanation: Preferential removal of low energy photons causes beam hardening. In a uniform object this can produce cupping, with spuriously low central CT numbers, and streaks near dense structures.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Uses a thicker filter.
stems.explanation: CT uses substantial shaped filtration, including a bow tie filter, to harden and shape the beam across the patient.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Filtered backprojection refers to a technique involving using a filter to remove low energy beams.
stems.explanation: The filter in filtered backprojection is a mathematical convolution filter applied to projection data before backprojection. It is not physical x ray filtration.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Slice thickness affects dose.
stems.explanation: As a direct setting: slice thickness mainly affects noise and z-resolution unless mAs is changed.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Adjusting window width can improve contrast.
stems.explanation: Narrowing window width increases displayed contrast by spreading a smaller HU range across the grey scale.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Metal can cause photon starvation occurs in the centre.
stems.explanation: Dense metal can attenuate nearly all photons along some paths, producing photon starvation and streak artefact.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Multislice detectors don’t get ring artifact.
stems.explanation: A faulty or miscalibrated detector element can still create ring artefact in multidetector CT.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Water has HU of 0.
stems.explanation: Water is defined as 0 HU.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Air has HU of -100.
stems.explanation: Air is around -1000 HU; -100 HU is closer to fat.

stems.label: B
stems.text: MPR of isotropic image can produce an oblique image without loss of quality.
stems.explanation: Near isotropic voxels allow multiplanar reconstruction in oblique planes with little or no loss of spatial resolution relative to the source data.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Objects at periphery may appear brighter than at the centre.
stems.explanation: Vignetting causes reduced brightness at the image intensifier periphery, not increased brightness.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Barium enema has a DAP of 45-50Gycm-2.
stems.explanation: DAP is dose multiplied by irradiated area and helps estimate stochastic risk.

stems.label: B
stems.text: 1µGymm-2 = 1cGym-2.
stems.explanation: Check the unit conversion carefully; DAP conversions require both dose prefix and area conversion to be handled together.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Dose of CT head is 1-3mSv.
stems.explanation: A typical adult non contrast CT head effective dose is of the order of 1 to 3 mSv, although protocol and scanner values vary.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Something about an ionisation chamber with a thin 0.5mm window can measure beta-particle emission dose.
stems.explanation: Beta dosimetry needs an appropriate thin-window detector; the vague recalled chamber statement is not a reliable CT dose statement.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Referrer must justify the examination.
stems.explanation: The referrer supplies clinical information; the practitioner justifies the exposure.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Practitioners must be doctor/dentists.
stems.explanation: An IR(ME)R practitioner must be adequately trained and entitled by the employer. The role is not restricted solely to registered doctors or dentists.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Operator is responsible for optimising dose.
stems.explanation: Under IR(ME)R, the operator optimises the practical exposure within their assigned duties, while the practitioner justifies the exposure.

stems.label: A
stems.text: RPA must design local rules.
stems.explanation: The employer establishes local rules after consulting the Radiation Protection Adviser. The Radiation Protection Supervisor helps implement them.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Employer is responsible to ensure employees are compliant.
stems.explanation: The employer must provide arrangements, training and supervision to ensure compliance with radiation safety requirements.

stems.label: C
stems.text: All employees entering the area must be immediately classified.
stems.explanation: Entering a controlled area does not automatically make a worker classified; classification depends on likely occupational dose and work pattern.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Objects 3mm apart can be resolved.
stems.explanation: Routine gamma camera spatial resolution is closer to about 10 mm clinically, so objects only 3 mm apart are not usually resolved.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Collimator’s primary function is to remove scatter.
stems.explanation: The gamma-camera collimator primarily provides spatial information by accepting photons from selected directions; energy-windowing is the main scatter rejection method.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Higher resolution than planar imaging.
stems.explanation: If saying superior spatial resolution: SPECT has better localisation/contrast but not necessarily better spatial resolution than planar imaging.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Higher contrast than planar imaging.
stems.explanation: SPECT improves contrast by separating overlying/underlying activity with tomographic reconstruction.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Higher dose than planar imaging.
stems.explanation: SPECT reconstructs a 3D activity distribution from rotating gamma camera projections.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Better attenuation correction.
stems.explanation: SPECT can use attenuation correction, especially with CT-based correction.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Detects positron annihilation within the nucleus.
stems.explanation: Positron annihilation occurs after the positron leaves the nucleus and meets an electron.

stems.label: B
stems.text: 2D acquisition is done with collimators.
stems.explanation: PET detects paired 511 keV annihilation photons in coincidence.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Minimum coincidence timing window depends on distance between detectors and speed of light.
stems.explanation: Coincidence timing requirements are related to photon travel time and detector timing resolution. Time of flight localisation uses the arrival time difference between opposing detectors.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Have a high chemical purity.
stems.explanation: High chemical and radiochemical purity ensures the activity is in the intended compound and limits unwanted biodistribution.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Long half life.
stems.explanation: An ideal diagnostic radiopharmaceutical should have a half-life long enough for imaging but short enough to minimise dose; a long half-life is undesirable.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Emit energy 100-250keV.
stems.explanation: Ideal diagnostic gamma photon energy is roughly 100-250 keV, balancing tissue escape with collimator and detector efficiency.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Emit some beta particles.
stems.explanation: Beta emission adds absorbed dose without helping external gamma-camera imaging; an ideal imaging radionuclide is a gamma emitter with little particulate emission.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Acoustic impedence directly proportional with density.
stems.explanation: Acoustic impedance is Z = rho c, so it is directly proportional to tissue density.

stems.label: B
stems.text: 99% of ultrasound reflected at air-soft tissue interface.
stems.explanation: The air-soft tissue impedance mismatch reflects almost all ultrasound; gel removes the air interface.

stems.label: C
stems.text: 15% of ultrasound reflected at soft tissue-fluid interface.
stems.explanation: Reflection at a soft tissue fluid interface is usually very small because their acoustic impedances are similar, generally well below 15 percent.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Maximum when beam is parallel to blood flow.
stems.explanation: Doppler shift increases with blood velocity.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Change in ultrasound velocity when it is reflected.
stems.explanation: Doppler effect is the change in frequency of the ultrasound echoes when reflected by a moving object. True: Doppler shift increases with blood velocity.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increase in ultrasound frequency when reflected by blood moving towards probe.
stems.explanation: Doppler shift is directly proportional to transmitted frequency.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Susceptibility is taken advantage of in T2* weighted imaging.
stems.explanation: Susceptibility artefact arises from local magnetic field distortion and spin dephasing.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Turbulent flow is bright on GRE.
stems.explanation: GRE is fast but more susceptible to T2* and magnetic field inhomogeneity because it lacks a 180 degree pulse.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Chemical shift can occur in the frequency-encoding direction.
stems.explanation: Fat-water frequency differences are mapped as displacement along the frequency-encoding axis.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Voxel size.
stems.explanation: Increasing voxel volume includes more spins in each voxel and increases signal. For fixed matrix size, a larger field of view or thicker slice therefore increases SNR.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Matrix size.
stems.explanation: Increasing matrix size at fixed FOV makes pixels smaller, so each pixel contains less signal and SNR falls.

stems.label: C
stems.text: TR.
stems.explanation: A longer TR allows more longitudinal recovery before the next excitation, increasing signal and SNR, although scan time increases.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Receiver bandwidth.
stems.explanation: Increasing receiver bandwidth increases noise admitted per pixel, so SNR decreases; narrower bandwidth improves SNR but increases chemical shift artefact.

stems.label: E
stems.text: TE.
stems.explanation: A longer TE allows more T2/T2* decay before signal sampling, so SNR decreases rather than increases.

stems.label: A
stems.text: STIR is used with gadolinium contrast to produce a useful image.
stems.explanation: STIR suppresses tissues by T1 and can also suppress gadolinium enhanced tissue. Frequency selective fat suppression is preferred after gadolinium when enhancement must remain visible.

title: Regarding MRI in and out of phase imaging

stems.label: A
stems.text: MRI in and out of phase imaging.
stems.explanation: In-phase and opposed-phase imaging exploits the cyclical phase difference between fat and water protons and is useful for detecting microscopic fat.

stems.label: A
stems.text: MRI safe means an item with demonstrated safety in MRI environment within defined conditions.
stems.explanation: That wording defines MR Conditional. MR Safe means the item poses no known hazards in any MR environment.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increases with slice thickness.
stems.explanation: Slice thickness and field of view are not simple primary determinants of SAR. SAR is dominated by RF pulse amplitude, flip angle, pulse number, duty cycle, patient loading and field strength.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increases with flip angle.
stems.explanation: SAR rises approximately with the square of RF flip angle because larger excitation requires more RF power.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Microbubbles work by having a diameter equal to wavelength of ultrasound beam.
stems.explanation: Microbubbles are only a few micrometres in diameter, much smaller than the ultrasound wavelength; their nonlinear oscillation creates strong contrast echoes.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Lead is used as a protective agent because of its high atomic number.
stems.explanation: Lead's high atomic number and density provide strong attenuation, particularly through photoelectric absorption at lower photon energies.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Gadolinium cannot be used if eGFR <30.
stems.explanation: If absolute: gadolinium is avoided or used with caution in eGFR <30 depending on agent and indication.

stems.label: A
stems.text: 1g of bone will have more absorbed dose then 1g of soft tissue.
stems.explanation: For the same incident photon fluence, bone may absorb more energy than soft tissue because photoelectric absorption is greater, so absorbed dose can be higher. The exposure conditions must be the same.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The characteristic radiation energy is much lower than the initial electron energy.
stems.explanation: The recall key marks this true: characteristic x-ray energy is set by shell binding-energy differences, while the incident electron or photon energy used to create the vacancy is usually higher.

title: Regarding USS heating at the particular point will depend on

stems.label: A
stems.text: USS heating coefficient.
stems.explanation: Local temperature rise depends on absorbed acoustic energy and on heat transfer away by conduction and perfusion.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Blood flow in the tissue.
stems.explanation: Perfusion carries heat away, so local ultrasound heating depends on tissue blood flow as well as absorbed acoustic power.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Transfer of heat within the tissue.
stems.explanation: Local temperature rise depends on heat conduction/perfusion away from the exposed region.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Cryogen is a flammable hazard.
stems.explanation: Helium is inert and non flammable. Its major hazards are cold injury, pressure and oxygen displacement during a quench.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Distance of controlled area is 0.5mT.
stems.explanation: The MR controlled access boundary is conventionally associated with the 0.5 mT, or 5 gauss, fringe-field contour.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The magnet is the biggest hazard.
stems.explanation: The static field is always present and creates projectile/implant hazards; gradients, RF heating and cryogens add further risks.

stems.label: A
stems.text: 90 degree RF pulse is used.
stems.explanation: Conventional spin echo starts with a 90 degree excitation pulse.

stems.label: B
stems.text: 180 degree RF pulse is used.
stems.explanation: The 180 degree refocusing pulse rephases spins and produces the spin echo.

stems.label: C
stems.text: It is possible to get T2* effect.
stems.explanation: Spin echo produces true T2 weighting; T2* effects are characteristic of GRE.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Having more phase encoding steps improves signal due to longer TE.
stems.explanation: Longer TR. Spin echo uses 90 degree excitation and 180 degree refocusing, making it less sensitive to susceptibility than GRE.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Scatter to transmission ratio is 10:1.
stems.explanation: Scatter can greatly exceed transmitted primary radiation in large fields; a 10:1 scatter-to-primary/transmission ratio is a possible high-scatter situation, not a universal constant.

stems.label: A
stems.text: High Pulse Repetition Frequency (PRF) is limited by depth of tissue measured.
stems.explanation: The next pulse cannot be sent until echoes return from the selected depth, so maximum PRF is limited by imaging depth.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Sampling frequency must be twice the frequency to avoid aliasing.
stems.explanation: This is the Nyquist rule. Pulsed Doppler must sample at least twice the Doppler frequency shift to avoid aliasing.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Aliasing is more likely when the blood flow is 30cm per second.
stems.explanation: Aliasing can occur even at physiological velocities if PRF is too low, especially with deep sampling or high transmitted frequency.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Inversely proportional to density.
stems.explanation: Doppler shift depends on transmitted frequency, reflector velocity and cosine angle.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Inversely proportional to compressibility.
stems.explanation: Doppler shift depends on transmitted frequency, reflector velocity, insonation angle and sound speed, not tissue compressibility.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Speed in tissue is affected by temperature.
stems.explanation: Sound speed can vary with temperature because material stiffness and density change.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Speed in tissue is 1240ms-1.
stems.explanation: Diagnostic ultrasound systems assume an average soft-tissue speed of about 1540 m/s; 1240 m/s is too low for typical soft tissue.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Only radiologist can justify scans above 5mSV.
stems.explanation: Justification depends on employer entitlement and training, not on a 5 mSv threshold or the person being a radiologist.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Gaseous waste is not considered radioactive waste.
stems.explanation: Radioactive gases and patient excreta can constitute radioactive waste and must be managed under the applicable authorisation and local procedures.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Local Councils will inspect the premises to see if it adheres to the rules.
stems.explanation: Radioactive substances and waste regulation is handled by the relevant environmental regulator, not ordinary local council inspection.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Waste produced by patients is not considered radioactive waste.
stems.explanation: Patient excreta may contain radioactivity after nuclear medicine administration, but management depends on activity, isotope, route and local waste rules.

title: Regarding size of effective focal spot is affected by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Target angle.
stems.explanation: Smaller focal spots reduce penumbra and improve geometric sharpness.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Size of filament.
stems.explanation: Filament size and electron focusing help determine the effective focal spot size at the anode.

stems.label: C
stems.text: mA.
stems.explanation: Blooming. True: smaller focal spots reduce penumbra and improve geometric sharpness.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Grids improve spatial resolution.
stems.explanation: Grids mainly improve contrast by absorbing scatter; they do not improve intrinsic spatial resolution.

title: Regarding MRI signal to noise ratio is improved by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Size of field of view.
stems.explanation: Increasing voxel volume includes more spins in each voxel and increases signal. For fixed matrix size, a larger field of view or thicker slice therefore increases SNR.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Bigger slice selection.
stems.explanation: A thicker selected slice contains more excited spins, so signal and SNR increase, at the cost of slice resolution.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Narrower receiver bandwidth.
stems.explanation: Narrowing receiver bandwidth reduces noise per pixel and improves SNR, although it increases chemical shift and susceptibility-related distortions.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Bigger pixel size.
stems.explanation: Larger pixels/voxels contain more spins, increasing signal and SNR but reducing spatial resolution.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Bigger matrix size.
stems.explanation: For a fixed FOV, a bigger matrix gives smaller pixels, reducing voxel signal and SNR.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Signal to noise ratio is increased in DSA, after subtracting the mask image.
stems.explanation: Subtraction combines noise from the mask and live images, so image noise increases and SNR decreases unless dose or temporal averaging is increased.

title: Regarding spatial resolution in USS is affected by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Turning up TGC.
stems.explanation: Changing gain or monitor brightness changes displayed amplitude, not the intrinsic spatial resolution of the ultrasound system.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Turning up the brightness of the monitor.
stems.explanation: Monitor brightness changes display appearance, not the intrinsic axial or lateral resolution of the ultrasound beam.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Higher frequency.
stems.explanation: Higher frequency shortens wavelength and improves axial resolution, but penetration is reduced.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Dose to patient is increased if radionuclide has longer physical half life.
stems.explanation: When other factors are unchanged. A longer physical half life increases residence time and total nuclear transformations, raising absorbed dose.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Bone scan is 0.5mSV.
stems.explanation: A typical adult technetium bone scan effective dose is several mSv, commonly around 3 to 4 mSv, not 0.5 mSv.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Positron is detected by coincidence detectors.
stems.explanation: PET detects paired 511 keV annihilation photons in coincidence.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Cyclotrons are on hospital site.
stems.explanation: Some centres have onsite cyclotrons, but many receive short lived PET radionuclides from a regional production site.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Field of view of gamma camera is determined by size of collimator holes.
stems.explanation: Gamma camera field of view is mainly determined by the usable crystal and detector area, not by individual collimator hole size.

stems.label: B
stems.text: In Tc99m high sensitivity collimator is preferred to higher resolution collimator.
stems.explanation: Collimator choice depends on the examination. A high resolution collimator is often selected for technetium 99m when detail is important; high sensitivity is not universally preferred.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Molybdenum 68 is the parent of Tc99m. False. Parent is Mo99.
stems.explanation: Mo-99, not Mo-68, is the parent radionuclide in a Mo-99/Tc-99m generator.

title: Regarding desirable characteristics of radionuclide are

stems.label: A
stems.text: More than 500keV. False. Would prefer 150keV to 400keV.
stems.explanation: Diagnostic gamma photons above 500 keV are too penetrating and cause septal penetration; useful energies are typically much lower, around 100-250 keV.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Can be bound to a suitable pharmaceutical.
stems.explanation: The radionuclide must be attachable to a suitable pharmaceutical that localises in the target organ.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Half life more than 12 hours. False. Most used radionuclide is Tc99m which half life is 6 hours.
stems.explanation: For an ideal general diagnostic radionuclide: the half-life should be long enough for imaging but short enough to minimise dose; Tc-99m is about 6 hours.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Accumulates in the target organ.
stems.explanation: An ideal radiopharmaceutical should localise in the organ or process being imaged to maximise target-to-background contrast.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Produces Beta radiation. False. Gamma radiation is desired.
stems.explanation: Diagnostic nuclear medicine generally wants gamma emission for external detection; beta particles mainly increase local absorbed dose.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Film dosimeters can measure both Beta and gamma radiation.
stems.explanation: A film badge with appropriate filters can estimate exposure from beta, x ray and gamma radiation within its energy response.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Thermodosimeters can be used to measure finger doses.
stems.explanation: Thermoluminescent dosimeters/ring dosimeters can monitor extremity doses such as finger dose in radionuclide work.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Electronic dosimeters are not sensitive enough for IR.
stems.explanation: Electronic personal dosimeters can be sensitive enough for instantaneous/real-time monitoring in interventional radiology; TLDs/OSLs are used for official dose records.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Thermolumunicent dosimeters sensitivity is 0.1mSV.
stems.explanation: TLD sensitivity depends on design and readout; 0.1 mSv is not a safe universal sensitivity statement for all TLD dosimeters.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Effective dose requires knowledge of tissue weighting factor.
stems.explanation: Effective dose uses tissue weighting factors to estimate whole-body stochastic risk.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Is the same as the whole body equivalent dose for the same stochastic risk.
stems.explanation: Effective dose is defined as the uniform whole-body equivalent dose that would carry the same overall stochastic risk as the actual non-uniform exposure, via the tissue weighting factors.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is relatively the same for most tissues in the diagnostic range of energies.
stems.explanation: Compton scatter involves a loosely bound outer-shell electron and is the dominant interaction in soft tissue at diagnostic energies.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Phosphor life is affected by radiation heat.
stems.explanation: CR phosphor plate life is limited mainly by handling damage, scratches, dirt and ageing, not by radiation heating.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Spatial resolution is better then film.
stems.explanation: For CR. Screen film historically had higher limiting spatial resolution, while CR offers wider dynamic range and processing flexibility.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Can be read after a 12 hours to a week.
stems.explanation: The latent image on a CR plate fades with time, so plates should be read promptly rather than left for many hours or days.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Comparing flat panel detectors with image intensifiers, FPD has lower geometric distortion.
stems.explanation: Flat panel detectors have much less pincushion and magnetic distortion than image intensifiers.

stems.label: A
stems.text: In beam hardening, lowers the CT number in the middle of the image.
stems.explanation: Beam hardening removes low-energy photons and can cause cupping or low central CT numbers.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Water HU number is 100.
stems.explanation: Water is defined as 0 HU; +100 HU is soft-tissue/blood range, not water.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Ring artefact can occur in multislice CT.
stems.explanation: Ring artefact can occur in multislice CT when a detector element is miscalibrated or faulty.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increasing pitch, decreases dose.
stems.explanation: Pitch affects dose, scan time and noise; dose is inversely related to pitch if other factors are fixed.

stems.label: B
stems.text: In cone beam effect, the artefact is at the centre of the axis.
stems.explanation: Cone beam artefact is greatest away from the central plane, where the x ray beam is most oblique to the detector rows.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The RPS has to do prior risk assessment once pregnancy is notified.
stems.explanation: The employer must review the risk assessment and working conditions after pregnancy is declared; the RPS assists locally but is not the legal duty holder.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Dose limit of fetus is 1mSV from date it is informed in writing.
stems.explanation: Once pregnancy is declared in writing, working conditions must make it unlikely that the fetal dose exceeds 1 mSv during the remainder of pregnancy.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Must avoid fluoroscopy.
stems.explanation: Pregnant staff do not automatically have to avoid fluoroscopy or radiopharmaceutical work. Duties are modified according to risk assessment, monitoring, time, distance and shielding.

stems.text: Reconstruction.
stems.explanation: When referring to iterative reconstruction. It can preserve image quality at a lower acquisition dose, although reconstruction itself does not alter radiation already delivered.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Does storage increase with larger matrix sizes.
stems.explanation: Larger matrices contain more pixels, so storage requirements increase.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Spatial resolution better than film screen.
stems.explanation: Film-screen mammography/radiography can have higher intrinsic spatial resolution than many digital detector systems.

stems.label: A
stems.text: IRR is concerned with quality assurance of equipments.
stems.explanation: IRR protects workers and the public. Medical equipment quality assurance for patient exposures is addressed under IR(ME)R and employer procedures.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Employer should maintain an invoice of the equipments.
stems.explanation: The employer must maintain an equipment inventory, QA programme and procedures; an invoice is not the relevant radiation-safety record.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Effective dose can be calculated from DAP.
stems.explanation: DAP is dose multiplied by irradiated area and helps estimate stochastic risk.

stems.label: D
stems.text: AP CXR conversion factor more than in PA projection.
stems.explanation: An AP chest projection generally irradiates radiosensitive anterior tissues more directly than PA, so its effective dose conversion factor is higher.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Local DRL should be set for all the examinations undertaken.
stems.explanation: This is false because the word 'all' is too absolute. Local diagnostic reference levels should be established for appropriate standard examinations or procedures where dose data can be meaningfully compared, particularly common or higher dose work. They are not required as a separate numerical level for every individual examination undertaken.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Accepted range of ESD in fluoroscopy 10-50mGy.
stems.explanation: As written because entrance surface dose in fluoroscopy must be expressed as a dose rate. The intended quantity is of the order of 10 to 50 mGy per minute, depending on patient size, equipment and operating mode, rather than 10 to 50 mGy without a time denominator. A cumulative entrance dose would depend on the duration of fluoroscopy.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Medico legal exposures included in IRMER.
stems.explanation: Non medical imaging exposures, including certain medico legal exposures, are included within IR(ME)R where the regulations apply.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Referrer needs to be informed about the dose involved.
stems.explanation: As a universal duty statement: the referrer supplies clinical information; dose/risk communication follows employer procedures and practitioner/operator roles.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Quality assurance carried annually.
stems.explanation: As a blanket statement: QA includes constancy tests at intervals set by the programme; some checks are much more frequent than annually.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Risk of developing fatal childhood cancer is 1in 3000 per 1mSv.
stems.explanation: The commonly recalled excess childhood cancer risk is closer to 1 in 13,000 per mSv, not 1 in 3,000 per mSv.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Stocheastic effects - no threshold.
stems.explanation: Radiation protection assumes no threshold for stochastic effects, with probability rather than severity increasing with dose.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Lens of the eye is measured as an equivalent dose.
stems.explanation: The lens is radiosensitive and cataract/lens opacity is a deterministic tissue reaction.

stems.label: A
stems.text: ARSAC holder can prescribe in all the hospitals he/she works.
stems.explanation: An ARSAC practitioner licence and employer certificate are tied to specified practices and sites. Authority is not automatically transferable to every hospital where the practitioner works.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Dose to children is half of the adult dose.
stems.explanation: Paediatric administered activity is scaled using weight or validated paediatric dosage cards, not simply fixed at half the adult activity.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Breast feeding should be stopped for 24hrs.
stems.explanation: Mammography uses low-energy spectra, compression and high spatial resolution while minimising glandular dose.

stems.label: D
stems.text: NM examinations are contraindicated in a pregnant patient.
stems.explanation: Pregnancy is not an automatic absolute contraindication; the examination must be justified, optimised and usually deferred if not urgent.

stems.label: E
stems.text: All radioactive waste has to be disposed in sacks.
stems.explanation: Radioactive waste disposal route depends on waste form, isotope, activity and local/environmental permit conditions; it is not all disposed of in sacks.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Wedging to test kV.
stems.explanation: A step wedge assesses contrast/receptor response; kVp accuracy is tested with a calibrated kVp meter.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Contrast detail test objects used for fluoroscopy.
stems.explanation: Contrast detail test objects assess the ability of a fluoroscopy system to display low contrast objects of different sizes.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Fluoroscopy unit is affected by magnetic fields.
stems.explanation: If referring to the whole fluoroscopy unit; the image intensifier component is the part susceptible to magnetic distortion.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Fluoroscopy image intensifiers are affected by magnetic fields.
stems.explanation: For image intensifiers: external magnetic fields deflect electron paths and distort the image.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Fluoroscopy unit is affected by metal casing.
stems.explanation: The casing itself is not the recognised cause of image distortion; magnetic fields affecting electron trajectories are the relevant problem.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The output of tube measured annually.
stems.explanation: This is false according to the testing schedule in the uploaded FRCR Physics Notes. X ray tube output is tested every one to two months using an ionisation chamber at a known distance and a range of exposures. An annual interval is therefore too infrequent for the schedule given in the reference, although local quality assurance programmes may assign additional formal annual tests.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Can pass through unaffected.
stems.explanation: An x ray photon may traverse matter without interacting.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Can disappear completely.
stems.explanation: A photon may be completely absorbed in a photoelectric interaction, transferring its energy to an electron.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Divert from direction and gain energy.
stems.explanation: In Compton scatter the photon changes direction and loses energy to the recoil electron; it does not gain energy.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Back scattered photon of 180 gains more energy.
stems.explanation: At 180-degree backscatter the photon loses the greatest energy and the recoil electron gains the greatest energy.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Intensity dependent on kV.
stems.explanation: X ray output increases approximately with kVp squared when mAs is unchanged.

title: Regarding effective focal spot is affected by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Anode disc diameter.
stems.explanation: Effective focal spot is governed mainly by actual focal spot and target angle, not anode disc diameter.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Target material.
stems.explanation: Target material affects X-ray production/spectrum, not the geometric effective focal spot size.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Anode-cathode distance.
stems.explanation: Anode-cathode distance does not define effective focal spot; filament/focusing and target angle do.

title: Regarding focal spot size increases by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Target angle.
stems.explanation: Increasing the target angle increases the effective focal spot size, while reducing target angle reduces effective focal spot but worsens anode heat loading/coverage.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Target material.
stems.explanation: Target material affects X-ray production/spectrum, not the geometric effective focal spot size.

stems.label: A
stems.text: CS predominates.
stems.explanation: Compton scatter predominates in soft tissue at typical CT photon energies.

stems.label: B
stems.text: PEE predominates.
stems.explanation: Photoelectric absorption completely absorbs the photon and ejects a bound electron; characteristic radiation may follow.

stems.label: C
stems.text: HU of fat is typically -100.
stems.explanation: Fat is typically around -50 to -100 HU.

stems.label: D
stems.text: HU are given depending on the density of the material.
stems.explanation: CT number depends on linear attenuation, which is influenced by physical density, atomic number and photon energy.

stems.label: E
stems.text: If an object is smaller than the pixel size it is not seen.
stems.explanation: A subpixel object may still be visible through partial volume averaging if it produces sufficient contrast, although it cannot be spatially resolved at its true size.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Radioactive decay - emits radiation.
stems.explanation: Radioactive decay is spontaneous nuclear transformation accompanied by particulate or electromagnetic radiation.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Physical half life should be 24 hrs.
stems.explanation: An ideal diagnostic radionuclide should have a short practical half-life; 24 hours is unnecessarily long for many studies and increases dose.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Gamma ray energy should be 300KeV.
stems.explanation: As an ideal fixed value. Diagnostic gamma photons are preferably around 100 to 250 keV; 300 keV increases septal penetration and reduces collimator efficiency.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Parent should have shorter life than the daughter.
stems.explanation: Mo-99, not Mo-68, is the parent radionuclide for Tc-99m generators.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Can be produced in cyclotron.
stems.explanation: Several imaging radionuclides, including F-18 and I-123, are produced in cyclotrons.

stems.label: A
stems.text: PHA reduces noise.
stems.explanation: The pulse height analyser accepts events within an energy window around the photopeak, rejecting many scattered lower energy events and improving contrast.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Size of the crystal affects spatial resolution.
stems.explanation: Gamma camera crystal thickness/light spread affects intrinsic resolution; thicker crystals improve sensitivity but can worsen resolution.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Collimator holes affect spatial resolution.
stems.explanation: Hole diameter, length and septal thickness determine the collimator resolution and sensitivity trade off.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Photomultiplier does not affect the number of electrons.
stems.explanation: PMTs convert scintillation light to electrical pulses and help localise the event; they do not optically focus light.

stems.label: A
stems.text: If Transducer surface has high temperature it is due to increase in voltage.
stems.explanation: Probe surface heating mainly reflects electrical and mechanical losses within the transducer and poor acoustic coupling. It is not explained simply by increasing voltage.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Due to friction.
stems.explanation: Ultrasound heating is mainly from absorption of acoustic energy, not mechanical friction in the everyday sense.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Local heating mainly due to energy absorption.
stems.explanation: Tissue heating occurs when absorbed ultrasound energy is converted into heat.

stems.label: D
stems.text: TI is the increase in temp by 2 degrees.
stems.explanation: TI estimates tissue temperature rise and is affected by tissue attenuation, especially near bone.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increases echoes from behind the fluid filled structures.
stems.explanation: TGC can amplify deeper echoes generally, but posterior acoustic enhancement behind fluid is a propagation effect caused by reduced attenuation, not a specific TGC function.

stems.label: B
stems.text: It can be altered to increase the echoes from structure behind the fluid filled structures.
stems.explanation: As a statement about the control, although it does not explain posterior acoustic enhancement. Time gain compensation can be adjusted for a selected depth range and therefore can increase the displayed amplitude of echoes from structures behind a fluid filled structure. Natural posterior enhancement is caused by reduced attenuation through fluid, and inappropriate TGC may either exaggerate or compensate for that appearance.

stems.label: C
stems.text: In Abdomen scanning 99% of time is utilised in receiving the echoes.
stems.explanation: Pulse echo ultrasound spends most of each pulse repetition period listening for returning echoes, commonly around 99 percent.

title: Regarding 21 operator can control - in US

stems.label: A
stems.text: PRF.
stems.explanation: The operator can alter pulse repetition frequency within limits imposed by imaging depth and mode.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Frame rate.
stems.explanation: The operator can alter frame rate indirectly through depth, sector width, line density and focal zones.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Focal zone.
stems.explanation: The operator can set focal zone position/number, which changes lateral resolution and frame rate.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Safety values for inner controlled area - 3mT.
stems.explanation: The MR Controlled Access Area is conventionally associated with the 0.5 mT, or 5 gauss, static field contour. Some guidance also defines an inner controlled area at 3 mT.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Controlled Area: >0.5 mT (5 Gauss).
stems.explanation: The MR Controlled Access Area is conventionally taken from the 0.5 mT, or 5 gauss, static field contour.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Inner Controlled Area: 3 mT.
stems.explanation: Some MR safety guidance uses 3 mT for an inner controlled area, so this is a recognised safety boundary value.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Person responsible for maintaining controlled areas "MR Responsible Person".
stems.explanation: The MR Responsible Person implements local MR safety procedures and controls access; the MR Safety Expert gives specialist advice.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Person with pacemaker is not allowed to enter 0.5mt stray field area.
stems.explanation: As an absolute statement. A person with an MR Unsafe or unverified pacemaker must not enter the MR environment, but many modern cardiac implantable electronic devices are MR Conditional and may enter under the manufacturer's specified conditions and an approved local protocol. The 0.5 mT contour defines the MR environment and triggers screening; it is not a universal ban on every pacemaker.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Whole body SAR restricted to 1 degree.
stems.explanation: In concept: normal operating mode SAR limits are designed to keep whole-body temperature rise around 1 degree Celsius.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Pregnancy - 1st trimester is an absolute contraindication.
stems.explanation: First-trimester pregnancy is not an absolute contraindication to MRI, but the scan must be justified and gadolinium avoided unless essential.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Uses a bipolar gradient.
stems.explanation: Gradient echo forms the echo by reversing the readout gradient, using dephasing and rephasing gradients rather than a 180-degree RF refocusing pulse.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Small flip angles.
stems.explanation: GRE commonly uses small flip angles and short TR, making it fast and relatively low SAR.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Short repetition times (TR).
stems.explanation: GRE often uses short TR because the flip angle is usually less than 90 degrees and no 180-degree refocusing pulse is required.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Low SAR.
stems.explanation: GRE generally has lower SAR than spin echo because it avoids repeated 180-degree RF refocusing pulses.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increases with increasing field strength.
stems.explanation: Chemical shift increases at higher B0 because the absolute frequency separation increases.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Decreased by increasing bandwidth.
stems.explanation: Increasing receiver bandwidth reduces the pixel displacement from chemical shift.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Affected by using gadolinium contrast.
stems.explanation: Gadolinium shortens T1 but does not remove the fat-water resonance frequency difference.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Occurs in frequency encoded direction.
stems.explanation: Fat-water frequency differences are mapped as displacement along the frequency-encoding axis.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Always occurs in pahse encoding direction.
stems.explanation: Chemical shift is due to the 3.5 ppm resonance difference between fat and water.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The nucleus contains equal numbers of protons and neutrons
stems.explanation: This is approximately true for atoms with Z<20, but the number of neutrons starts to increase for Z >20. Also, the hydrogen nucleus contains no neutrons at all.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The K-shell can hold up to 8 electrons
stems.explanation: The K-shell can only hold up to 2 electrons

stems.label: C
stems.text: All the electrons have negative energy in the atom
stems.explanation: Negative energy means they are 'bound' to the atom and can’t escape without receiving energy from an outside source, such as an x-ray.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The binding energy of the K-shell is proportional to the mass number of the nucleus
stems.explanation: The binding energy increases with the atomic number, Z, rather than the mass number. Even so, the increase in BE is not linear.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Chemical properties of the atom are determined by the number of electrons in the outermost shell
stems.explanation: Valence shell electrons participate in chemical bonding and determine the chemical properties of an element

title: The photoelectric effect in x-ray studies

stems.label: A
stems.text: Only occurs with K-shell electrons
stems.explanation: It can also occur in the L-shell or M-shell

stems.label: B
stems.text: Can produce characteristic radiation
stems.explanation: Characteristic radiation is emitted when an electron drops into the vacancy left behind by the photoelectron

stems.label: C
stems.text: Creates subject contrast in planar radiography
stems.explanation: The rate at which PE occurs is very sensitive to the differences in atomic number (Z) between adjacent tissues, resulting in large differences in x-ray beam attenuation (ie subject contrast)

stems.label: D
stems.text: Occurs less frequently at higher tube currents (mA)
stems.explanation: The likelihood of the photoelectric effect (PE) occurring depends on the energy of the xrays in the beam. Tube current (mA) only effects the number of x-rays emitted, not their energy.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Does not occur in the patient during CT scanning
stems.explanation: Although Compton scatter is the predominant interaction in the patient, PE does occur infrequently (eg an x-ray may undergo multiple scattering events which will reduce its energy, followed by a PE event)

stems.label: A
stems.text: Occurs between an x-ray and a free electron
stems.explanation: CS occurs when the binding energy of the electron is a negligible fraction of the x-ray energy. This is typically the case for outer shell electrons which are furthest from the nucleus and have very low BE.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The energy transferred to the electron increases with increasing scattering angle
stems.explanation: The x-ray loses more energy when scattered through a wide angle. This energy is transferred to the electron.

stems.label: C
stems.text: At higher incident x-ray energies, the energy of the scattered radiation also increases
stems.explanation: Scattered x-rays carry away a portion of the incident energy. As the energy of the incident photon increases so does the energy of the scattered photons.

stems.label: D
stems.text: It does not occur in bone for x-ray photons with energy below 45keV
stems.explanation: It is less prevalent than the photoelectric effect, but it still occurs.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is the dominant interaction in soft tissue in nuclear medicine studies
stems.explanation: Photon energy in nuclear med studies is typically > 100keV & at this energy Compton scattering is the dominant interaction in soft tissue.

title: The effective focal spot of an x-ray tube

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is equal in size to the area of target from where x-rays are emitted
stems.explanation: The area of target from where x-rays are emitted is the 'real' focal spot size. The effective spot size is the projection of this onto the patient or image receptor. The effective focal spot size is smaller due to the target angle (line focus principle).

stems.label: B
stems.text: Decreases with increasing target angle
stems.explanation: Small target angles produce small effective focal spots

stems.label: C
stems.text: Depends on the size of the cathode filament
stems.explanation: Different filament sizes are used to create ‘broad’ & ‘fine’ focal spots

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is typically 1.0mm in conventional units
stems.explanation: Most units have a broad focal spot size of 1.2mm and a fine focal spot size of 0.6mm

stems.label: E
stems.text: Limits the contrast of the acquired image
stems.explanation: Focal spot size influences geometric unsharpness, but does not affect contrast. Contrast is determined by x-ray interactions in the patient and so depends on the kVp and the composition & thickness of the patients tissues.

title: Increasing the kVp of an x-ray tube from 60 to 80 will

stems.label: A
stems.text: Require the tube current (mA) to be reduced by approximately one-half to deliver the same dose to the image receptor
stems.explanation: With a patient in the beam the receptor dose rises roughly as kV⁴, so the mAs must fall by about a factor of 3 — "one half" only holds free-in-air (kV²).

stems.label: B
stems.text: Reduce the relative number of photoelectric interactions that take place in the patient
stems.explanation: Probability of PE interaction decreases rapidly with increasing x-ray energy. Average x-ray energy in the beam is proportional to the tube voltage, kVp

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increase the image contrast
stems.explanation: Image contrast is created by photoelectric interactions in the patient. The relative number of these interactions will be lower at 80kVp

stems.label: D
stems.text: Reduce the amount of scattered radiation reaching the image receptor
stems.explanation: Relatively more scatter events will occur at 80kVp. This scatter will have more energy than it would at 60kVp and a greater proportion will be directed toward the receptor. Hence, more scatter is likely to reach the image receptor at 80kVp

stems.label: E
stems.text: Reduce the entrance surface dose to the patient for the same receptor dose
stems.explanation: At 80kVp a greater proportion of the beam will penetrate through the patient & reach the image receptor. Therefore, a lower entrance surface dose will be possible at 80kVp while still maintaining the same dose to the receptor.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The image plate is not sensitive to background radiation
stems.explanation: Any ionising radiation is capable of exposing the image plate.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Post-processing algorithms are selected according to the radiographic projection
stems.explanation: Digital images are produced in CR, which can be post-processed to promote visualisation of specific features in different studies.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The thickness of the phosphor layer is limited by the need to minimise read-out laser light spread
stems.explanation: A thicker phosphor will absorb more x-ray energy, making the plate more sensitive. However, the laser light used to read out the image plate will undergo greater amounts of scatter in a thick phosphor and this will degrade spatial resolution.

stems.label: D
stems.text: An inappropriately low exposure may result in increased image noise
stems.explanation: For low exposures, fewer x-rays will be used to form the image. This will increase image noise.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The image plate consists of a matrix of individual detector elements
stems.explanation: The image plate is a uniform phosphor coated onto a supporting plate. The discrete sampling of the signal during the read-out process produces a digital image.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The brightness gain is the product of the flux gain and the minification gain
stems.explanation: Brightness gain = flux gain x minification gain

stems.label: B
stems.text: The brightness gain is typically 5000-10000
stems.explanation: Brightness gain = flux gain x minification gain. Flux gain is typically 50-100 and the minification gain is typically ~100

stems.label: C
stems.text: The minification gain is numerically equal to the ratio of the diameters of the input and output screens
stems.explanation: Minification gain = area of the input screen / area of output screen. The area of each screen is proportional to square of its diameter.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The falloff in brightness towards the edge of the image intensifier is referred to as veiling glare
stems.explanation: The fall off in brightness towards the edge of the image intensifier is known as 'vignetting'

stems.label: E
stems.text: In magnification mode the limiting spatial resolution and contrast ratio both improve
stems.explanation: Spatial resolution and contrast are improved but at the expense of increased patient dose

title: Concerning gamma camera imaging with Tc99m

stems.label: A
stems.text: Tc99m decays by electron capture
stems.explanation: Tc99m decays via isomeric transition

stems.label: B
stems.text: Tc99m emits a gamma ray with energy of 0.14 MeV
stems.explanation: Tc99m emits gamma rays at 140keV (which is the same as 0.14MeV)

stems.label: C
stems.text: There is no associated β-particle emission
stems.explanation: Tc99m emits gamma rays, but not beta particles

stems.label: D
stems.text: The detection efficiency of the scintillator crystal is of the order of 40%
stems.explanation: The NaI crystal in a gamma camera absorbs ~90% of any Tc99m gamma rays

stems.label: E
stems.text: The effective half-life of the tracer is dependent upon the radiopharmaceutical used
stems.explanation: The effective half-life depends on both the physical half-life of the radionuclide and the biological half-life of the radiopharmaceutical

title: The contrast in a planar nuclear medicine scan is dependent

stems.label: A
stems.text: The type of collimator fitted to the gamma camera
stems.explanation: Collimators determine sensitivity & spatial resolution, but have no effect on contrast.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The separation between the patient & collimator
stems.explanation: Changing the separation between the patient & collimator will affect spatial resolution only. (The air gap technique does not work in nuclear medicine because both the primary & scattered radiation is emitted in all directions).

stems.label: C
stems.text: The width of the pulse height analyser window
stems.explanation: The width of the pulse height analyser window will control the amount of scatter being recorded in the image. Wider PHA windows allow more scatter into the image. Scatter always reduces contrast.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The delay between injection and scan
stems.explanation: Contrast in nuclear medicine depends on the relative uptake of the radioactive tracer in different organs. A delay between injection and scanning allows for greater biological clearance of the tracer from background tissues.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The radiochemical purity of the radiopharmaceutical
stems.explanation: Contrast in nuclear medicine depends on the relative uptake of the radioactive tracer in different organs. Radiochemical purity of the radiopharmaceutical refers to the % of total radioactivity that is bound to the pharmaceutical. So a radiochemical purity of 90% means 10% of the administered activity is 'unbound' and will be taken up by different organs than the administered radiopharmaceutical. Hence, the radiochemical purity (or labelling efficiency) will affect the relative distribution of the tracer within the patient, and therefore the contrast.

title: Regarding planar bone scanning in nuclear medicine

stems.label: A
stems.text: Spatial resolution deteriorates with increasing distance from the collimator
stems.explanation: Gamma camera collimators are very 'short-sighted'. Spatial resolution deteriorates with increasing distance from the collimator.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The spatial resolution of the images is typically 10mm FWHM
stems.explanation: This is a typical value for planar whole-body bone scans

stems.label: C
stems.text: The activity can only be administered by a practitioner with an ARSAC license
stems.explanation: Administration can be performed by a trained IRMER operator (eg a radiographer) following a written protocol.

stems.label: D
stems.text: There is a legal limit of 600MBq on the injected activity
stems.explanation: 600MBq is the national DRL for planar bone scanning. The DRL can be exceeded in individual circumstances provided the additional exposure is justified by the IRMER practitioner.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The effective dose to the patient is typically 3mSv
stems.explanation: This is the calculated effective dose to an average sized patient following the administration of 600MBq Tc99m-phosphonates

stems.label: A
stems.text: Typically require the administration of larger activities than planar studies
stems.explanation: The administered activity is increased to improve image quality (SPECT reconstruction amplifies random noise)

stems.label: B
stems.text: Are acquired using high resolution collimators for studies involving Tc99m
stems.explanation: High resolution collimation is needed to compensate for the increased separation between camera & patient in a SPECT study (which deteriorates spatial resolution).

stems.label: C
stems.text: Are degraded by photon attenuation in the patient
stems.explanation: Photon attenuation causes an apparent reduction in the intensity of deeper structures compared to more superficial ones and must be corrected for.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Are degraded by gamma camera non-uniformity
stems.explanation: Gamma camera non-uniformity can cause ring artefacts in SPECT images

stems.label: E
stems.text: Have poorer spatial resolution than planar studies
stems.explanation: SPECT studies are acquired at greater collimator-patient separations than planar studies, leading to degraded spatial resolution. Also SPECT reconstruction results in additional smoothing/blurring of the images. However, SPECT images have much better contrast than planar images.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Sodium iodide is typically used as the detector crystal
stems.explanation: Sodium iodide is not very efficient at detecting the 511keV gamma rays in PET. Instead, BGO, LSO or GSO are frequently used as scintillators in PET scanners.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The sensitivity of the scanner for detecting radiation is much higher than for SPECT cameras
stems.explanation: The sensitivity is higher in PET because collimators (which absorb most of the radiation) are not used

stems.label: C
stems.text: Both positrons & gamma radiation are detected
stems.explanation: PET scanners do not detect positrons; they detect annihilation radiation (511keV gamma rays)

stems.label: D

title: Concerning the biological effects of ionising radiation

stems.label: A
stems.text: Induction of malignancy is a deterministic effect
stems.explanation: Deterministic effects (or tissue reactions) only occur above a relatively high threshold dose. The severity of the effect increases with dose (above the threshold). They also appear very quickly after exposure. Cancer induction does not meet these criteria and is a stochastic effect.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The cornea is more radiosensitive than the lens

stems.label: C
stems.text: Medical exposures in the first trimester of pregnancy increases the likelihood of the foetus having Down's syndrome

stems.label: D
stems.text: A single dose of 2 Gy to the eye may cause point opacities in the lens
stems.explanation: Cataract formation is a deterministic effect (or tissue reaction) with a threshold dose of ~0.5Gy

stems.label: E
stems.text: Gamma-rays have a higher radiation weighting factor than x-rays
stems.explanation: X-rays and gamma-rays both have a radiation weighting factor of 1

stems.text: The primary function of a bow tie filter is to reduce the appearance of streak artifacts from metal implants

stems.text: Beam hardening artifacts commonly occur at bone-soft tissue junctions
stems.explanation: Bone preferentially absorbs low energy x-rays due to its high atomic number (Z) and mass density. As low energy ("soft") photons are removed form the beam, the average photon energy will increase, making it more penetrating ("harder").

stems.label: C
stems.text: Partial volume artifacts can be reduced by increasing the pitch
stems.explanation: The partial volume artifact refers to the averaging of signals from multiple different tissues within pixels. Measured signals are averaged during spiral CT. As the pitch increases more averaging occurs, making partial volume effects more likely.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The calculated CT number of any tissue is independent of the X-ray tube voltage (kVp)

stems.label: E

title: Spatial resolution in CT imaging can be improved by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Using a smaller focal spot size
stems.explanation: Using a smaller focal spot size reduces geometric unsharpness

stems.label: B
stems.text: Sampling the transmitted x-ray signal using smaller x-ray detectors
stems.explanation: Smaller detectors offer improved spatial sampling of the transmitted x-ray beam, which will improve the spatial resolution

stems.label: C
stems.text: Decreasing the scan time
stems.explanation: Decreasing the scan time reduces the possibility of patient motion artifacts

stems.label: D
stems.text: Interpolating the final image from a 512x512 matrix to a 1024x1024 matrix
stems.explanation: Interpolation occurs after the data has been acquired. The spatial resolution cannot be improved beyond the detector size used to sample the transmitted x-ray beam during acquisition. Interpolation reduces the apparent size of pixels in the image (to make them less noticeable), but because it occurs after the acquisition, it does not improve spatial resolution.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing the slice thickness
stems.explanation: Increasing the slice thickness will reduce spatial resolution along the axial direction, leading to greater partial volume artifacts (blurring of signal).

title: The noise recorded in a CT study is increased

stems.label: A
stems.text: By increasing the matrix size
stems.explanation: Increasing the matrix size (eg from 256x256 to 512x512) will make the pixels smaller. The number of photons recorded in each pixel will therefore decrease, hence random/Poisson noise will increase.

stems.label: B
stems.text: When imaging obese patients
stems.explanation: There will be greater attenuation of the beam, which will reduce the number of x-rays reaching the detectors hence, random noise will increase.

stems.label: C
stems.text: By decreasing the gantry rotation speed
stems.explanation: Decreasing the gantry rotation speed (fewer rotations per second) will increase the the number of x-rays emitted per slice of the study and therefore decrease the noise.

stems.label: D
stems.text: By increasing the tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: Increasing the tube current will increase the number of x-rays emitted per rotation and therefore decrease the noise (because more x-rays are detected per CT slice).

stems.label: E
stems.text: By decreasing the display window width
stems.explanation: Decreasing the display window width will enhance the visualisation of small differences in image intensity. Noise may become more apparent, but the actual level of noise recorded in the image will not change.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is measured in units of mGy/cm
stems.explanation: CTDI is measured in mGy

stems.label: B
stems.text: Is the dose delivered to the organs of the patient
stems.explanation: CTDI is the average dose in a standard-sized Perspex phantom. It can be used to compare radiation doses for different imaging protocols.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increases with tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: CTDI is directly proportional to tube current (mA)

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increases with the pitch of the scan
stems.explanation: Both CTDI and patient dose decrease with increasing pitch for spiral CT scans (CTDIvol= CTDI/pitch)

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is higher for head scans than for body scans when using the same scan parameters
stems.explanation: A 32cm diameter phantom is used to measure CTDI for body imaging. A 16cm diameter phantom is used to measure CTDI for head imaging. Due to the smaller phantom size for head scans, there is less attenuation causing the dose along the central axis of the phantom to increase.

title: Patient doses delivered during CT imaging

stems.label: A
stems.text: Are proportional to the tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: Increasing the mA will increase the mAs, which is proportional to the number of x-rays interacting with (& delivering a dose to) the patient.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Are proportional to the gantry rotation speed
stems.explanation: Patient dose is directly proportional to the mAs. Increasing the gantry speed will reduce the acquisition time per slice and therefore the mAs. Hence patient dose will decrease.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increase with the pitch of the scan
stems.explanation: As pitch increases, there are increasing gaps between consecutive CT slices. Hence, the x-ray beam passes through a smaller volume of tissue. The patient dose therefore decreases.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Can be reduced using iterative reconstruction techniques
stems.explanation: Iterative reconstruction (IR) can reduce the noise in a reconstructed image. Therefore, IR permits lower exposure parameters to be used (which would normally increase noise), without any overall increase in noise. Using lower exposure parameters will reduce patient dose.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Are typically 4mSv effective dose for a study of the abdomen & pelvis
stems.explanation: 8mSv would be more typical for a CT study of the abdomen & pelvis

title: In MR imaging, the Larmor frequency is

stems.label: A
stems.text: The rate at which protons precess in a magnetic field
stems.explanation: Protons will precess at the Larmor frequency in a magnetic field.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Proportional to the field strength, Bo
stems.explanation: A proton will precess twice as fast in a 2T field compared to a 1T field

stems.label: C
stems.text: Proportional to the T1 relaxation time
stems.explanation: T1 is a measure of how quickly the longitudinal magnetisation recovers after a 90 degree pulse. It does not affect the Larmor frequency.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Inversely proportional to the gyromagnetic ratio
stems.explanation: Larmor frequency is proportional to the gyromagnetic ratio. Different nuclei have different gyromagnetic ratios.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Decreases with time due to relaxation processes
stems.explanation: Relaxation processes govern the behaviour of the MR signal, not the Larmor frequency of individual protons.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The bulk magnetisation vector, Mo represents a single proton precessing about the axis of the main magnetic field, Bo
stems.explanation: Mo represents the collective behaviour of the proton spin population.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The magnitude of Mo is independent of the strength of Bo
stems.explanation: Mo is directly proportional to Bo

stems.label: C
stems.text: After a 90 degree RF pulse the longitudinal and transverse magnetisation vectors are equal in size
stems.explanation: After a 90 degree pulse the longitudinal magnetisation vector, Mz=0, while the transverse magnetisation vector, Mxy=Mo

stems.label: D
stems.text: After a 180 degree RF pulse the nuclear spin population will be inverted
stems.explanation: A 180 degree pulse will invert the spin population. Note that the protons themselves are not physically relocated just the phase of their spin.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Rotation of the magnetisation vector in the x-y plane gives rise to the MR signal
stems.explanation: A rotating magnetisation vector will induce a voltage in a receiver coil

title: During the spin echo pulse sequence

stems.label: A
stems.text: After the 90 degree RF pulse, magnetic field inhomogeneities cause the protons to lose phase coherence
stems.explanation: This is true, but dephasing also occurs due to intermolecular spin-spin interactions

stems.label: B
stems.text: The 180 degree RF pulse rephases the spins
stems.explanation: Rephasing the spins creates an echo signal at a time TE/2 after the 180 degree pulse

stems.label: C
stems.text: The spin echo signal appears at a time TE after the 180 degree pulse
stems.explanation: The MR signal (echo) appears at time TE after the 90 degree pulse

stems.label: D
stems.text: It can be used to generate either T1 or T2 weighted images
stems.explanation: T1 or T2 weighted images can be generated by choosing appropriate values for TR (pulse repetition time) & TE (time to echo).

stems.label: E
stems.text: Multiple sequential 180 degree pulses can be applied after the 90 degree pulse to improve the contrast in T1-weighted images
stems.explanation: Multiple 180 degree pulses are used in FSE (Fast Spin Echo) sequences where contrast is compromised for faster imaging

stems.label: A
stems.text: Frequently use flip angles < 90 degrees
stems.explanation: A small flip angle allows greater recovery of the longitudinal magnetisation vector, Mz between repeated pulse excitations. This allows shorter pulse repetition intervals (TR) and faster scans.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Apply a 180 degree RF pulse to generate the MR signal
stems.explanation: A bipolar gradient field is used to dephase & subsequently rephase the spin population to generate an “echo” signal.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Can be used to generate T2-weighted images
stems.explanation: GRE sequences produce T2* weighted images (ie as well as the T2 relaxation time of the tissues, the inhomogeneity of the main magnetic field also contributes to the decay of the MR signal).

stems.label: D
stems.text: Are often used for MR angiography
stems.explanation: GRE is a fast imaging procedure that can be used to generate blood flow studies

stems.label: E

stems.label: B
stems.text: In bone, travel at greater than twice the speed compared to soft tissue

stems.label: C

stems.explanation: Tissues with a high collagen content are strong absorbers of US radiation

stems.label: D

title: Regarding the interaction of US beams with human tissue

stems.label: A
stems.text: The intensity of a beam decreases exponentially with depth
stems.explanation: US radiation undergoes exponential attenuation in tissue. This means a fixed fraction of the beam energy is removed per cm travelled

stems.label: B
stems.text: Both reflection & refraction can occur at the junction of two tissues with differing acoustic impedances
stems.explanation: Both processes can occur when there is a change in acoustic impedance, but refraction will only occur if the beam strikes the interface at an oblique angle

stems.label: C

stems.label: D
stems.text: US radiation does not interact with structures that are smaller than the wavelength of the US pulse
stems.explanation: US radiation is scattered by objects that are smaller than the wavelength

stems.label: E

stems.explanation: Quoted values range from 0.5 1.0 dB/cm/MHz

title: The axial resolution of an ultrasound image depends on

stems.label: A
stems.text: The diameter of the transducer crystal
stems.explanation: This will change the width of the beam line & so will affect lateral resolution, rather than axial resolution.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The pulse repetition frequency (PRF)
stems.explanation: PRF is the number of pulses emitted per second. This will not affect axial resolution.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Focusing of the US beam
stems.explanation: Beam focusing will change the width of the beam line & so will affect lateral resolution, rather than axial resolution.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The spatial pulse length (SPL)
stems.explanation: Spatial pulse length (number of waves in each pulse x wavelength) directly affects axial resolution. Axial resolution = SPL/2

stems.label: E
stems.text: The depth of the target in the patient
stems.explanation: Axial resolution = Spatial pulse length (SPL) / 2. The SPL does not change with depth, so axial resolution is independent of depth.

title: Regarding the Doppler Effect in US imaging

stems.label: A
stems.text: The frequency of reflected US waves decreases for objects moving towards the transducer
stems.explanation: The frequency increases for objects moving towards the receiver

stems.label: B
stems.text: The effect is greatest for structures moving at right angles to the direction of the US beam
stems.explanation: The effect is most noticeable when the beam is in the same direction as the motion

stems.label: C
stems.text: It requires a higher frequency than B-mode studies
stems.explanation: The same range of frequencies are used for both B-mode & Doppler

stems.label: D

stems.label: E

stems.text: The efficiency of bremsstrahlung emission is typically 10% in diagnostic x-ray tubes
stems.explanation: In diagnostic radiology only about 1% of the electron energy striking the target is emitted as bremsstrahlung x-rays

stems.text: Bremsstrahlung production is more efficient at higher tube voltages

So for an electron transition between the M-shell and the K-shell, the energy of the characteristic x-ray will be: X-ray energy = BE K-shell BE M-shell So the characteristic x-ray will always have slightly lower energy than the BE of the electron shell it was emitted from

title: The following actions will improve the spatial resolution of an

stems.label: A
stems.text: Decreasing the focal spot size from 1.6mm to 0.6mm

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing the tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: Increasing the mA (in isolation) will not improve resolution. Increasing the mA may allow for a shorter exposure time (which would reduce patient motion blur), however, the question didn't mention any change in exposure time.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Using an anti-scatter grid with a higher grid ratio
stems.explanation: Using a higher grid ratio will improve contrast (by removing scatter) but will affect not spatial resolution.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increasing the amount of added filtration in the beam
stems.explanation: Filtration changes the energy spectrum of the beam by preferentially removing low energy x-rays (which will affect contrast & patient dose), but will have no effect on spatial resolution.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Decreasing the patient-to-image receptor distance
stems.explanation: Decreasing the patient-to-image receptor distance will reduce geometric unsharpness (ie reduce the size of the penumbra around structures). In routine radiography the image receptor is positioned as close as possible to the patient.

title: Increasing the tube voltage of a diagnostic x-ray set will

stems.label: A

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increase the entrance skin dose (ESD) in direct proportion
stems.explanation: The ESD will increase, but not in direct proportion. ESD will increase according to the square of the kV

stems.label: C
stems.text: Reduce the effective dose to the patient if the image receptor dose is kept constant

stems.text: Increase the exposure time if the image receptor dose is kept constant
stems.explanation: The exposure time (mAs) can be REDUCED — the higher-kV beam is both more intense and more penetrating, so the same receptor dose arrives in a shorter time.

stems.label: E

stems.explanation: Increasing kVp (in isolation) will mean that more x-rays are emitted. Their energy is also increased so a greater proportion reach the image receptor, so image noise will decrease
