stems.label: D
stems.text: Characteristic x-rays must be filtered out of the beam
stems.explanation: High & low energy bremsstrahlung x-rays are filtered out of the beam using K-edge filtration. The energy of the characteristic x-rays is just right to maximise image contrast and these are preferentially transmitted by the k-edge filter.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Screening is justified because breast tissue has a low radiosensitivity
stems.explanation: The breast is radiosensitive, but screening is justified because asymptomatic lesions can be detected (and treated) at fairly low radiation doses, ie there is a net benefit to the exposure.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Tc99m is supplied by eluting a molybdenum generator each morning
stems.explanation: The Mo99-Tc99m generator is eluted each morning to provide a fresh supply of Tc99m

stems.label: B
stems.text: Tc99m gamma rays have a HVL of approximately 5cm in soft tissue
stems.explanation: This means that radiation emitted from a depth of 10cm will be attenuated by a factor of ~75%

stems.label: C
stems.text: Tc99m gamma rays predominantly interact with soft tissue via Compton scattering
stems.explanation: Tc99m gamma rays have an energy of 140keV which favours Compton scattering interactions in low Z materials (soft tissue).

stems.label: D
stems.text: The thickness of the scintillation crystal in a gamma camera affects both its spatial resolution & sensitivity
stems.explanation: Thicker crystals have better sensitivity (ie detect more radiation) but poorer spatial resolution

stems.label: E
stems.text: The width of the pulse height analyser window will affect both the contrast resolution & sensitivity of the gamma camera
stems.explanation: The PHA window controls the amount of scatter reaching the image. A wide PHA window allows more scattered radiation to be detected (so sensitivity will increase), however increased scatter will reduce image contrast.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Longer acquisition times will reduce image noise
stems.explanation: Longer acquisition times will allow more gamma rays to be detected, which reduces random (Poisson) noise

stems.label: B
stems.text: Dynamic studies are seldom performed
stems.explanation: Dynamic imaging is frequently used in renal, lymphatic and gastrointestinal studies.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The injected activity for thyroid imaging using Tc99m is typically 80MBq
stems.explanation: 80MBq is the national DRL specified by ARSAC. In a normal patient 1-4% of this activity will localise in the thyroid gland.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Using a high resolution collimator will allow shorter acquisition times
stems.explanation: High resolution collimators have reduced sensitivity and so allow fewer gamma rays to be detected each second. Hence, longer acquisition times are needed to acquire a pre-defined number of counts.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The spatial resolution in a bone scan image changes with increasing delay between administration of the radiopharmaceutical & scan acquisition
stems.explanation: Increasing the delay will allow greater clearance of tracer from background tissues. This will affect image contrast, not spatial resolution.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Reducing the angular sampling interval will improve the spatial resolution of SPECT images
stems.explanation: Decreasing the angular sampling interval form say 6-degrees to 3-degrees will increase the number of projections recorded in the SPECT study. Spatial resolution improves with increasing number of angular samples (projections).

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing the matrix size from 128x128 to 256x256 will improve the spatial resolution of SPECT images
stems.explanation: Changing the matrix size would improve resolution if pixel size was the limiting factor. In SPECT studies, the spatial resolution of the camera is very poor, so making the pixels smaller will not alter the sharpness of the images.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Spatial resolution is uniform throughout transaxial PET images
stems.explanation: Spatial resolution is optimum at the centre of transaxial images (ie along the central axis of the detector rings) and degrades slightly towards the periphery.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Spatial resolution in PET is better than that in SPECT
stems.explanation: Spatial resolution in PET is typically 4mm FWHM, while SPECT is ~10mm FWHM

stems.label: E
stems.text: In PET studies, the bed positions must be overlapped by at least 33% to compensate for axial variations in sensitivity
stems.explanation: This is done to compensate for the triangular axial sensitivity profile in 3D PET (sensitivity is largest in the centre of the axial FoV and decreases linearly towards the boundary of the FoV)

stems.label: A
stems.text: Random coincidences do not affect image quality
stems.explanation: Random coincidences are mis-positioned events and therefore reduce image contrast and must be corrected for.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The CT dose is much larger than that delivered by the 18FDG
stems.explanation: The effective dose from CT is typically 4-5mSv, which is lower than the dose from FDG (typically 5-6mSv)

stems.label: C
stems.text: The injected activity of 18FDG for adults is typically 100MBq
stems.explanation: Most adults will be injected with 250-350MBq FDG (the actual dose is based on patient weight, typically 3.0 4.0 MBq per kg are administered)

stems.label: D
stems.text: The effective dose to adult patients from 18FDG administration is typically 6mSv
stems.explanation: For administered activities in the range 250-350MBq the effective dose will be 5-7mSv

stems.label: E
stems.text: An uptake time of 30 minutes is used to prevent excessive decay of 18F
stems.explanation: Uptake periods of 60min are used for to permit optimum uptake in lesions

stems.label: A
stems.text: Require employers to be registered prior to starting diagnostic x-ray work
stems.explanation: The employer must register with the HSE prior to starting x-ray imaging work

stems.label: B
stems.text: Specify dose limits for occupational & medical exposures
stems.explanation: Medical exposures are not subjected to dose limits

stems.label: C
stems.text: Do not apply to procedures involving unsealed radionuclides
stems.explanation: The regulations apply to occupational exposure to any type of ionising radiation

stems.label: D
stems.text: Place responsibility for providing protection on the radiation protection adviser (RPA)
stems.explanation: The employer is responsible for providing protection. The RPA advises the employer on matters of radiation safety & compliance with IRR17.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Require all doses to be kept as low as reasonably practicable (ALARP)
stems.explanation: Doses being ALARP refers to dose optimisation, which is a fundamental requirement of the regulations

stems.label: A
stems.text: Any person performing QC tests on medical radiation equipment is acting as an operator
stems.explanation: An operator is someone who carries out practical aspects of a patient exposure. The outcome of equipment testing could significantly affect patient exposures

stems.label: B
stems.text: The practitioner is legally responsible for all aspects of the exposure
stems.explanation: Each professional is individually responsible for their own role in any patient exposure. The practitioner's responsibility is to justify the exposure.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The patient must be informed when an unintended or accidental exposure has occurred
stems.explanation: This will depend on the Employer's duty of candour policy. IRMER17 doesn't specify that the patient must be informed of any unintended exposure.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The regulations do not permit the exposure of a person unless they will benefit from it directly
stems.explanation: Normal volunteers can be exposed as part of a research trial and may not benefit from the exposure (society as a whole may benefit though).

stems.label: E
stems.text: Nuclear medicine studies may only be performed if both the practitioner and the employer possess a valid licence
stems.explanation: The licensing scheme under IRMER requires both the practitioner and the nuclear medicine department (ie the Employer) to hold a valid licence.

title: Regarding the management of radioactive waste in diagnostic

stems.label: A
stems.text: Patients administered with Tc99m-labelled tracers are expected to excrete 40% of the administered activity in their urine
stems.explanation: Excretion factors are used to estimate radioactive discharges. It is assumed that 40% of all Tc99m administrations enter the hospital sewer

stems.label: B
stems.text: Radioactive urine from injected patients must be stored in delay tanks for up to 1 week before entering the sewer
stems.explanation: Radioactive urine is discharged directly to the sewer, where it is diluted with non-radioactive waste

stems.label: C
stems.text: Solid radioactive waste containing Tc99m is typically stored on-site for up to 1 week
stems.explanation: Storage for 1 week will allow the radioactivity to decay to background levels

stems.label: D
stems.text: Injected in-patients can only return to another hospital or nursing home if that organisation has a permit for the disposal of radioactive waste
stems.explanation: Hospitals are exempt from needing a permit if they receive small numbers of injected patients each year

stems.label: E
stems.text: The MPE is responsible for ensuring that hospitals comply with the conditions of their radioactive waste permit
stems.explanation: The Radioactive Waste Advisor (RWA) is responsible for ensuring compliance with the regulations

title: Regarding radiation risks from medical exposures

stems.label: A
stems.text: The average effective dose to the UK population from all sources of radiation is approximately 0.3mSv
stems.explanation: It is approximately 2.7mSv per year

stems.label: B
stems.text: Approximately 15-20% of the annual dose is due to medical exposures
stems.explanation: On average, about 0.4mSv per year is due to medical irradiation. This is 0.4/2.7 = 15% of the total

stems.label: C
stems.text: An effective dose of 10mSv carries with it a risk of cancer induction of 1 in 2000
stems.explanation: The risk factor for cancer induction is 1 in 20,000 per mSv (averaged over the whole population). A dose of 10mSv will carry a risk of 1 in 20,000/10 or 1 in 2,000.

stems.label: D
stems.text: A dose of 25mSv delivered to a foetus will double the risk of cancer in childhood
stems.explanation: The risk factor for cancer induction for in-utero irradiation is 1 in 13,000 per mSv. A dose of 25mSv carries a risk of 1 in 13000/25, or 1 in 520. This is similar to the natural incidence of childhood cancer (currently this is 1 in 500 in the UK)

stems.label: E
stems.text: Five CT exposures of the head within a 3 month interval can result in cataract formation in a patient
stems.explanation: The maximum dose to the eyes would be ~40mGy from a single CT scan of the head. Hence at least 12 studies would be needed to reach the dose threshold for cataract induction (500mGy).

title: The effective dose to a patient for a radiographic examination

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is the sum of the equivalent dose to each organ multiplied by their respective weighting factors
stems.explanation: Effective dose = sum of (organ dose x tissue weighting factor)

stems.label: B
stems.text: Is measured in mGy
stems.explanation: Effective dose is measured in units of mSv

stems.label: C
stems.text: Is calculated by averaging the entrance and exit doses
stems.explanation: Effective dose depends on doses to individual tissues and the corresponding tissue weighting factors. The entrance & exit dose are the dose in air at the points where the beam enters & leaves the patient's body respectively.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is indicative of the radiation dose to a foetus for a pregnant patient
stems.explanation: Effective dose is a measure of the overall risk to the patient. The equivalent dose to the uterus would be indicative of foetal dose.

stems.label: E
stems.text: It is used to determine the risk from both stochastic and deterministic effects
stems.explanation: Effective dose is a measure of risk for stochastic effects only. (Deterministic effects always occur if the threshold dose is exceeded).

stems.label: A
stems.text: Pre-patient collimation is employed to remove scattered radiation
stems.explanation: Pre-patient collimators limit the volume of tissue irradiated along the z-axis of the patient. A thin antiscatter grid sits permanently on top of the bank of detectors to remove scatter.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The focal spot size is typically 1mm
stems.explanation: CT tubes generally have a large focal spot of 1.2mm and a fine focal spot of 0.6mm

stems.label: C
stems.text: The primary function of the bow tie filter is used to harden the beam
stems.explanation: The bow-tie filter is used to modulate beam intensity across the patient & reduce patient dose

stems.label: D
stems.text: Transaxial images are reconstructed using filtered backprojection
stems.explanation: FBP is still widely used to reconstruct transaxial slices

stems.label: E
stems.text: Image contrast is largely determined by tissue density
stems.explanation: Compton scatter is the predominant mode of interaction in the patient, which is dependent on the (mass) density of the patient's tissues

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is proportional to the tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: Increased mA will reduce noise, but SNR is proportional to √mAs (ie the square root of the mAs)

stems.label: B
stems.text: Is inversely proportional to gantry rotation speed
stems.explanation: A slower gantry rotation speed will increase the number of x-rays emitted and detected per slice. This will reduce noise, but not in a linear manner.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increases with the pitch of the scan
stems.explanation: Increasing the pitch will increase the 'gaps' between successive slices. The patient is exposed to less radiation. This will increase image noise but reduce dose to the patient.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is unaffected by the reconstruction filter
stems.explanation: The reconstruction filter smooths the image, which will affect SNR

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is unaffected by the CT display window width
stems.explanation: The SNR of data recorded in the image does not depend on the way it is displayed

title: Concerning the effective dose to the patient in CT

stems.label: A
stems.text: It is unaffected by pixel size
stems.explanation: Changing pixel size in isolation will not affect patient dose.

stems.label: B
stems.text: It is unaffected by slice thickness
stems.explanation: Changing slice thickness in isolation will not affect patient dose

stems.label: C
stems.text: The CT dose index (CTDI) is the organ dose delivered per slice
stems.explanation: It is the dose to a standard size phantom and is used to compare imaging protocols

stems.label: D
stems.text: It increases with the number of slices acquired
stems.explanation: More tissue will be irradiated, so the DLP will increase

stems.label: E
stems.text: It is typically 1-2mSv for a routine brain scan
stems.explanation: This is the effective dose for a standard sized patient

title: Regarding CT studies of the thorax-abdomen-pelvis in adults

stems.label: A
stems.text: CT data are acquired as a spiral scan
stems.explanation: Spiral (helical) acquisitions allow a large section to be imaged in a short period of time.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The tube voltage is typically 80-100kVp
stems.explanation: Higher tube voltages are typically used for adults, usually 120kVp or above

stems.label: C
stems.text: The in-plane spatial resolution is typically 0.7lp/mm
stems.explanation: This is typical of modern scanners

stems.label: D
stems.text: The CT acquisition is started simultaneously with IV contrast administration
stems.explanation: There must be a delay between the administration of the contrast and the start of CT acquisition to allow the contrast to reach the organs of interest in either the arterial or venous phase.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The minimum slice thickness attainable is equal to the z-axis beam collimation
stems.explanation: Beam collimation refers to the width of the beam along the z-axis, which must cover all the detectors in the array. Slice thickness is determined by the detector thickness in the z-axis.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is produced following any RF pulse
stems.explanation: No signal will be produced after a single 180 degree pulse, or if the spin population is saturated (this can happen when 90 degree pulses are repeated at short TR intervals)

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increases with main field strength (Bo)
stems.explanation: Signal size increases because the bulk magnetisation vector, Mo, increases with Bo

stems.label: C
stems.text: Decreases in size with time
stems.explanation: The signal decays due to spin-spin (T2) relaxation

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is created by spinning hydrogen nuclei
stems.explanation: The rotation of billions of tiny magnetic nuclei creates a signal in a receiver coil

stems.label: E
stems.text: Consists of a voltage induced in a coil of wire
stems.explanation: A rotating magnetisation vector will induce a voltage in a receiver coil

title: Regarding relaxation times in MR imaging

stems.label: A
stems.text: T1 is typically 20-200ms for most tissues
stems.explanation: The typical range for T1 is 200-2000ms

stems.label: B
stems.text: T1 decreases with increasing magnetic field strength
stems.explanation: For the majority of biological tissues, the T1 relaxation time lengthens as the magnetic field strength (Bo) increases.

stems.label: C
stems.text: For any tissue, T1 is always longer than T2
stems.explanation: The MR signal (Mxy) decays away long before Mz recovers. The decay of Mxy is determined by T2 relaxation. The recovery of Mz is determined by T1 relaxation. So T2 < T1

stems.label: D
stems.text: The T2 relaxation time is a measure of how fast the MR signal decays
stems.explanation: The T2 of any tissue is the time taken (in msec) for the MR signal to decay to 37% of its full value

stems.label: E
stems.text: The T1 relaxation time influences the repetition rate of a spin echo pulse sequence
stems.explanation: TR is chosen to allow Mz to recover to a particular level before the pulse sequence is repeated. The recovery of Mz is dependent on T1 so the choice of TR also depends on T1

title: Spatial resolution of MR images is improved by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Decreasing the slice thickness
stems.explanation: Reducing the slice thickness will reduce the voxel size, which results in finer spatial sampling of the patient

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing the image matrix size
stems.explanation: A larger matrix size (eg going from 128x128 to 192x192) means there are more pixels covering the same field of view. Hence, pixel size will be smaller and spatial resolution will improve due to finer digital sampling of the MR signal.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Decreasing the field of view
stems.explanation: A smaller field view means the same number of pixels are used to sample a smaller region of the patient. Hence, pixel size will be smaller and spatial resolution will improve due to finer digital sampling of the MR signal.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increasing the main magnetic field strength
stems.explanation: Increasing Bo will increase the SNR, but will not have a direct effect on spatial resolution

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing the time to echo (TE)
stems.explanation: Increasing TE will reduce the SNR, but will not affect spatial resolution

stems.label: A
stems.text: Occurs for tissues containing fat and water
stems.explanation: Because of the local magnetic effects of orbiting electrons, protons in water and fat have slightly different Larmor frequencies when placed in a strong magnetic field. This is the basis of the chemical shift artefact

stems.label: B
stems.text: Is more prominent at high field strengths
stems.explanation: The difference in Larmor frequency between water & fat is enhanced at higher field strengths

stems.label: C
stems.text: Is minimised by the STIR pulse sequence
stems.explanation: The signal from fat is eliminated by STIR

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is visible along the frequency encode axis of the image
stems.explanation: Changes in frequency are related to linear position along the frequency encode axis. Hence, the chemical shift artefact causes fat and water to be placed in different positions along this direction.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is caused by inhomogeneities in the main field
stems.explanation: The artefact occurs because of differences in the intrinsic magnetic properties of protons in water and fat molecules

title: Regarding biological effects in MR imaging

stems.label: A
stems.text: Static magnetic field strengths of 5T and above can interfere with brain function
stems.explanation: There is no evidence of permanent biological effects < 8 T

stems.label: B
stems.text: Any metal object presents a projectile hazard in the fringe field of the scanner
stems.explanation: Only ferromagnetic objects (ie those containing iron, nickel or cobalt) will be strongly attracted towards the scanner bore and present a missile hazard.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Rapid gradient switching can cause peripheral nerve stimulation
stems.explanation: During the acquisition of an image slice, the three gradient fields are switched on and off very rapidly. A rapidly changing magnetic field can induce a rapidly changing electric current that is capable of nerve stimulation in patients.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The specific absorption rate (SAR) is a measure of tissue heating
stems.explanation: RF energy absorbed in the body causes an increase in temperature & this is quantified by the SAR

stems.label: E
stems.text: Metal implants may be affected by the magnetic fields of both the main field & the RF pulses
stems.explanation: A ferromagnetic implant can be made to move or rotate in the presence of the Bo field, while the selective absorption of the RF field in the metal can cause elevated temperatures and increase the risk of burning adjacent tissues

title: In ultrasound examinations, the acoustic impedance of a

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increases with the mass density of the tissue
stems.explanation: Acoustic impedance measures how much a medium resists the transmission of sound waves. Denser tissues, like bone, have molecules packed closely together and this contributes to higher acoustic impedance.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increases with the speed of propagation of the beam in the tissue
stems.explanation: Sound travels faster through stiffer, less compressible materials. This 'stiffness' also increases the acoustic impedance of the medium. Hence, acoustic impedance increases with the speed of sound.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Depends on whether the tissue is stationary or moving
stems.explanation: Acoustic impedance is an intrinsic property of the tissue regardless of its state of motion

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is measured in units of decibels (dB)
stems.explanation: dB are used to compare the relative intensity of waves (for instance for quantifying attenuation). Acoustic impedance is measured in units called Rayls

stems.label: E
stems.text: Muscle has a greater acoustic impedance than fat
stems.explanation: Muscle has a slightly higher density than fat, so its acoustic impedance will be slightly greater.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Multiple pulses are sent down a single scan line
stems.explanation: This is true for A-mode & M-mode scans, but not for B-mode

stems.label: B
stems.text: Real time images are produced
stems.explanation: Images are built up in real time and refreshed each second

stems.label: C
stems.text: The selected pulse repetition frequency (PRF) depends on the imaging depth
stems.explanation: It takes 13 microseconds for a pulse to travel to & from a structure 1cm from the transducer. Deeper structures require longer intervals between successive pulses, so the PRF must decrease to prevent pulses overlapping

stems.label: D
stems.text: Image brightness is dependent on the angle of the transducer relative to the organ surface
stems.explanation: This will effect the angle of incidence of the beam on a tissue boundary. The maximum echo strength is received from normal incidence/reflection

stems.label: E
stems.text: Image brightness is proportional to the acoustic impedance of the tissues
stems.explanation: Image brightness in B-mode scans is proportional to the echo intensity. This depends on the difference in acoustic impedance between adjacent tissues

title: Axial resolution in a B-mode scan

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is dependent on the spatial pulse length (SPL)
stems.explanation: SPL = US wavelength x No of waves in a pulse. Axial resolution = SPL/2

stems.label: B
stems.text: Varies with depth in the patient
stems.explanation: Axial resolution depends only on the spatial pulse length (SPL) which in turn, depends on the wavelength of the US wave. Wavelength doesn't change with depth.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Improves with increasing frequency
stems.explanation: The wavelength of the US waves (and therefore the SPL) is shorter at higher frequencies. Hence axial resolution improves with increasing frequency.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is dependent on the diameter of the transducer
stems.explanation: The diameter of the transducer does not influence the SPL and therefore does not affect axial resolution.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is typically 0.5-1mm
stems.explanation: Wavelengths in US are 0.3-1.0mm, which produce Spatial Pulse Lengths of 0.9-3mm. Remember, Axial resolution = SPL/2

title: The frequency shift in Doppler ultrasound

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increases with Doppler angle
stems.explanation: Doppler shift is greatest for angle=0 degrees and drops to zero as the angle approaches 90 degrees

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increases with operating frequency
stems.explanation: Increasing the operating frequency of the US waves causes a larger frequency shift in the reflected signal

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increases with the velocity of blood flow
stems.explanation: The Doppler frequency shift increases in proportion to the velocity of blood flow

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increases with the propagation velocity of the ultrasound beam
stems.explanation: The Doppler shift is inversely proportional to propagation velocity

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increases with pulse repetition frequency (PRF)
stems.explanation: The PRF determines the maximum frequency shift that can be detected before aliasing occurs. It does affect not the size of the frequency shift though.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is the energy needed to move an electron up to the next shell
stems.explanation: It is the energy needed to remove the electron from the atom

stems.label: B
stems.text: Is greatest for K-shell electrons
stems.explanation: They are closest to the nucleus and & experience a strong attractive force

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increases with atomic number
stems.explanation: As Z increases so does the attraction between the nucleus & the electrons

stems.label: D
stems.text: Influences the occurrence of photoelectric events
stems.explanation: PE cannot occur unless the photon energy > binding energy

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is typically 10-70eV for K-shell electrons
stems.explanation: It is typically 10-70keV

title: For x-ray interactions in soft tissue

stems.label: A
stems.text: The liberated electrons released can travel several cm in tissue
stems.explanation: Photoelectrons are relatively low energy & will have a range of < 2mm in tissue

stems.label: B
stems.text: The probability of a Compton scatter event occurring is proportional to the product of the electron density of the tissue and the x-ray energy
stems.explanation: The probability of CS events decreases slowly with increasing photon energy

stems.label: C
stems.text: At photon energies > 100keV attenuation in soft tissue is almost entirely due to incoherent scatter
stems.explanation: Incoherent scatter is another phrase for Compton scatter. CS predominant interaction >100keV in soft tissue.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Scattered x-rays are emitted equally in all directions for incident energies above 100keV
stems.explanation: There is less backscatter and more forward scatter at higher x-ray energies (or tube voltage, kVp)

stems.label: E
stems.text: Elastic scattering accounts for ~10% of the dose at diagnostic energies
stems.explanation: Elastic scattering occurs at low kV but does not transfer energy to the patient (so zero radiation dose)

title: Regarding beam filtration in conventional x-ray machines

stems.label: A
stems.text: Its primary purpose is to remove characteristic radiation emitted from the x-ray target
stems.explanation: Added filtration preferentially removes low energy bremsstrahlung radiation from the beam

stems.label: B
stems.text: Added filtration changes the maximum energy of x-rays in the beam
stems.explanation: The maximum x-ray energy is determined by the tube voltage (kVp) only

stems.label: C
stems.text: Inherent filtration is typically equivalent to 2mm Al
stems.explanation: Inherent filtration is typically equivalent to ~0.5mm Al

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increasing amounts of aluminium filtration is required at higher tube voltages
stems.explanation: As kVp increases the range of x-ray energies in the beam will also increase (max energy=kVp and min energy depends on filtration). Greater amounts of filtration are needed to increase the minimum x-ray energy in the beam. Typical values are 1.5mm Al for < 70kVp, 2.5mm Al for >70kVp

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing the amount of filtration will reduce both the intensity and the half-value layer (HVL) of the beam
stems.explanation: Additional filtration will increase the mean energy of the beam, so it will become more penetrating. HVL must therefore increase too. The intensity of the beam (the total energy/sec crossing unit are of the beam) will decrease though.

stems.label: A
stems.text: A larger matrix improves spatial resolution
stems.explanation: The matrix size refers to the number of pixels along the axes of the image. A larger matrix will reduce pixel size & improve spatial sampling

stems.label: B
stems.text: A smaller pixel depth improves image contrast
stems.explanation: Pixel depth refers to the number of detected x-rays that can be stored in a pixel. Reducing this may result in signal saturation which will decrease contrast

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increasing the number of photons recorded per pixel improves the SNR
stems.explanation: More detected photons will reduce noise, signal-to-noise ratio will increase

stems.label: D
stems.text: Structures smaller than the voxel size cannot be detected in the image
stems.explanation: High-contrast structures smaller than the voxel size can be detected, but there will be some partial volume averaging

stems.label: E
stems.text: Applying a low pass filter to an image will reduce its noise
stems.explanation: This will suppress high spatial frequencies, which are associated with image noise

stems.label: A
stems.text: A photoconductor converts x-rays into light
stems.explanation: A photoconductor converts x-rays into an electric current. (A phosphor coverts x-rays into light)

stems.label: B
stems.text: They have a wide dynamic range
stems.explanation: The dynamic range of an image receptor = largest detectable signal / smallest detectable signal. FPDs have a wide dynamic range, typically 10,000:1 this is one of the main advantages of digital detectors

stems.label: C
stems.text: Barium fluorohalide is frequently used for the photoconductive layer
stems.explanation: BaFBr is used as the phosphor in computed radiography (CR) imaging plates

stems.label: D
stems.text: They cannot be used for fluoroscopy
stems.explanation: FPDs can replace image intensifiers for digital fluoroscopy

stems.label: E
stems.text: The spatial resolution of indirect FPDs is restricted by screen blur
stems.explanation: Indirect FPDs have a phosphor layer overlying a matrix of diodes. Light diffusion in the phosphor limits spatial resolution of the detector.

title: Quantum noise in fluoroscopy can be reduced by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increasing the tube voltage (kVp)
stems.explanation: Quantum/random/Poisson noise is decreased when more x-rays are detected. An increase in kVp will increase the intensity & penetration of the beam so more x-rays will reach the image intensifier thus decreasing the quantum noise

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing the tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: An increase in mA will increase the intensity of the beam. More x-rays will therefore be detected, thus decreasing the quantum noise.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Removing the anti-scatter grid
stems.explanation: Removing the anti-scatter grid will increase the number of x-rays reaching the image intensifier & so will reduce quantum noise, (a lot of these x-rays will be scattered so contrast will be degraded)

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increasing the source-to-skin distance
stems.explanation: Increasing the source-skin distance will move the image intensifier further from the x-ray tube & so will reduce the intensity of the beam. This will mean that fewer x-rays will be detected and so quantum/random noise will increase.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Selecting a different dose control curve for the automatic brightness control (ABC)
stems.explanation: The ABC automatically controls the kVp and mA of the x-ray tube in fluoroscopy. Alternative dose control curves are available that offer different trade-offs between image quality & patient dose.

title: Contrast in an x-ray image is improved by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Decreasing the tube voltage (kVp)
stems.explanation: Decreasing the kVp will increase subject contrast by promoting photoelectric events in the patient

stems.label: B
stems.text: Decreasing the tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: Changing the mA will have no effect on the energy of the x-rays. Contrast is created by differential attenuation between different tissues. This depends on tissue composition (atomic number and density) and the energy of the x-rays (changes the relative frequency of photoelectric and compton scatter interactions)

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increasing the source-to-skin distance
stems.explanation: Increasing the source-to-skin distance will improve geometric unsharpness, but will have no effect on contrast

stems.label: D
stems.text: Reducing the area of the x-ray beam
stems.explanation: Reducing the area of the x-ray beam will reduce the volume of tissue irradiated & therefore reduce the amount of scatter produced. Scattered radiation always degrades contrast.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Using a grid
stems.explanation: Using a grid will decrease the amount of scattered radiation reaching the image receptor

stems.text: Tc99m decays by isomeric transition
stems.explanation: In isomeric transition the nucleus transitions from a metastable state to the ground state with the emission of gamma radiation.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Radionuclides that decay via electron capture cannot be imaged with a gamma camera
stems.explanation: X-rays are released during EC which can used for imaging. Also the daughter nucleus may be left in an excited state and will relax with the emission of gamma radiation.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Electron capture occurs in proton-rich radionuclides
stems.explanation: The captured inner shell electron combines with a proton to convert it into a neutron. This reduces the atomic number by 1

stems.label: D
stems.text: Positron emission occurs in proton-rich radionuclides
stems.explanation: A proton is converted into a positron and a neutron. The positron is emitted from the nucleus and the atomic number decreases by 1

stems.label: E
stems.text: Isomeric transition reduces the atomic number of the parent atom
stems.explanation: During isomeric transtion the daughter nucleus releases energy in the form of gamma radiation hence there is no the There is no change in atomic number

stems.text: The main role of the collimator is to reject scatter
stems.explanation: The collimator is the image forming component of the camera. Scatter rejection is performed electronically by the PHA window.

stems.label: B
stems.text: A sodium iodide crystal converts gamma radiation into light
stems.explanation: The NaI crystal absorbs gamma radiation and emits a small flash of blue light

stems.label: C
stems.text: The camera calculates the energy of each detected gamma ray
stems.explanation: The energy of each gamma ray must be calculated to allow scatter rejection to occur. Scattered radiation has a lower energy than primary radiation. By setting an energy "window" around the detected photopeak low energy scatter and high energy background radiation can be rejected from the image.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The width of the pulse height analyser window affects the sensitivity of the camera
stems.explanation: The PHA window is an energy window placed around the detected photopeak. A wider PHA window will allow more gamma rays each second to be added to the image (although these will include a large proportion of scattered gamma rays).

stems.label: E
stems.text: Photomultiplier tube malfunctions cause non-uniformity artefacts
stems.explanation: A faulty PM tube will produce a circular low signal defect on a flood image

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increasing the separation between the patient & gamma camera will decrease quantum mottle
stems.explanation: Moving away from the collimator will affect the spatial resolution, but not the sensitivity. Changes in sensitivity will affect quantum mottle.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Image magnification increases with distance from a parallel hole collimator
stems.explanation: There is a 1:1 correspondence between image & object size with a parallel hole collimator

stems.label: C
stems.text: The proportion of scattered radiation recorded in the image decreases with increasing administered activity
stems.explanation: The proportion of scatter is unchanged with activity

stems.label: D
stems.text: Signal-to-noise ratio increases with increasing administered activity
stems.explanation: This will increase the number of detected gamma rays, which reduces image noise so SNR improves

stems.label: E
stems.text: Radionuclide & radiochemical impurities in the administered radiopharmaceutical will affect image contrast
stems.explanation: Contrast depends on the relative organ uptake of the administered tracer. When impurities are present, the distribution of the radiopharmaceutical amongst different organs changes.

title: In positron emission tomography using fluorine-18

stems.label: A
stems.text: All the positrons are emitted with the same energy
stems.explanation: Positrons from F18 are emitted with a continuous range of energies up to a maximum value of 635keV

stems.label: B
stems.text: Rings of detectors are slowly rotated around the patient during image acquisition
stems.explanation: The detector rings are stationary during a PET acquisition

stems.label: C
stems.text: In-plane spatial resolution of reconstructed slices improves towards the centre of the FoV
stems.explanation: Spatial resolution is optimum at the centre of the FoV

stems.label: D
stems.text: In-plane spatial resolution of reconstructed slices is largely unaffected by the positron range in tissue
stems.explanation: Positron range can affect spatial resolution, but F18 positrons have a relatively short range in tissue and don't significantly degrade the resolution.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Random coincidences do not affect image contrast
stems.explanation: Random coincidences are mispositioned within the image, which adds a background 'fog' and reduces contrast

title: With regard to the standardised uptake value (SUV)

stems.label: A
stems.text: It is a simplified index of glucose utilisation
stems.explanation: FDG is a glucose analogue. The SUV is a measure of relative FDG uptake in organs compared to uniform distribution.

stems.label: B
stems.text: It assumes that the plasma concentration of FDG is proportional to the injected dose and inversely proportional to body weight
stems.explanation: SUV = tissue concentration of FDG (kBq/ml) / (Injected activity / patient mass)

stems.label: C
stems.text: It is independent of the type of PET scanner used
stems.explanation: SUV is affected by a number of different parameters, including scanner type

stems.label: D
stems.text: It is independent of uptake time (delay between injection & scan)
stems.explanation: SUV is based on the plasma concentration of FDG which will change with time

stems.label: E
stems.text: The calculation is influenced by the type of reconstruction algorithm used
stems.explanation: The type of algorithm used during reconstruction will affect the accuracy of any quantitative index (including SUV).

stems.text: They are designed to prevent the occurrence of tissue reactions
stems.explanation: They are set well below the dose thresholds for tissue reactions to occur

stems.label: B
stems.text: The effective dose limit always takes precedence over dose limits to individual organs
stems.explanation: There is no hierarchy for dose limits. It is illegal to exceed any dose limit.

stems.label: C
stems.text: It is illegal for a classified radiation worker to receive an equivalent dose of 25mSv to the lens of the eye in 1 year
stems.explanation: 20mSv is the annual dose limit for the lens of the eye. It is illegal to exceed any dose limit.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The annual dose to the hands of an unclassified worker must not exceed 150mSv
stems.explanation: 150mSv is the dose threshold at which classification is compulsory

stems.label: E
stems.text: The effective dose limit for a pregnant radiation worker is 1mSv
stems.explanation: The dose to the foetus is limited to 1mSv for the remainder of the pregnancy but the dose limit for the mother remains at 20mSv

title: With regard to the Ionising Radiation Medical Exposure

stems.label: A
stems.text: They do not apply to exposures incurred during health screening
stems.explanation: They apply to diagnosis, therapy, health screening, occupational health surveillance, medico-legal, research or any exposure of an asymptomatic individual.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Radiographers & nurses can act as a practitioner
stems.explanation: Any registered healthcare professional can be a practitioner, provided they have received appropriate training and have been entitled to do so by the employer.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Optimisation of an exposure means delivering a radiation dose sufficient to obtain the best image quality
stems.explanation: This would promote the use of high radiation doses. Optimisation means the dose used in the procedure is just enough to prvide relevant diagnostic information.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Justification of an exposure ensures the difference between risk and benefit of the procedure is maximized.
stems.explanation: Justification is the process for determining that a procedure will result in a net benefit. The question is referring to 'optimisation', where the operator ensures the smallest possible radiation exposure is adopted for the process.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Individual duty holders can be prosecuted if they breach the regulations
stems.explanation: Any duty holder named in IRMER may be prosecuted individually for failure to meet their obligations under the regulations.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Carries a risk of cancer induction of approximately 1 in 3000
stems.explanation: The risk factor for cancer induction for the general public is 1 in 20,000 per mSv. So a dose of 6mSv carries a risk of 1 in 20,000/6 = 1 in 3,300 (which is approximately 1 in 3,000)

stems.label: B
stems.text: Would be delivered to a patient during an chest CT scan
stems.explanation: The effective dose will be typically 5-8mSv for a CT scan of the chest

stems.label: C
stems.text: Is the dose threshold for classification of staff
stems.explanation: Staff must be classified radiation workers if they are likely to exceed 3/10 of any dose limit. 6mSv is ~3/10th of the annual effective dose limit (20mSv) for staff

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is ten times the average background radiation dose in the UK for one year
stems.explanation: The annual dose due to background radiation averaged across the UK is ~2.5mSv

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is the annual dose limit for members of the public
stems.explanation: 1mSv is the annual dose limit for members of the public

title: Regarding radiation protection in the Radiology Department

stems.label: A
stems.text: Lead aprons must be able to protect the wearer against primary and secondary xrays
stems.explanation: Lead aprons are not designed to protect the wearer against the primary beam

stems.label: B
stems.text: The dose rate due to scattered radiation at 1m from a patient is approximately 0.1% of the dose rate incident on the patient
stems.explanation: About 0.1% of the radiation incident on a patient will be scattered to staff standing 1m away (wearing a lead apron will protect against this dose though).

stems.label: C
stems.text: It is a legal requirement for all staff to receive training in radiation protection
stems.explanation: Training in radiation protection is a requirement of IRR17

stems.label: D
stems.text: Leakage radiation from x-ray tubes must not exceed 1mGy/hr at 1m from the focal spot
stems.explanation: Some radiation will always escape from an x-ray tube during operation. Restricting the dose rate to 1mGy/hr at 1m will help limit the dose to staff.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The inverse square law can be applied to x-ray machines
stems.explanation: The inverse square law (ISL) states that radiation from a small point source will be emitted equally in all directions. The intensity of the radiation will be inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source. The focal spot of an x-ray tube is small enough to be considered a “point” source, so the ISL will apply.

title: The calculated CT number of a pixel in a transaxial CT slice is

stems.label: A
stems.text: Tube voltage (kVp)
stems.explanation: The CT number (HU) is a measure of the attenuating properties of the tissue (relative to water) in the corresponding voxel in the patient. Attenuation properties change with x-ray energy, which is affected by the kVp

stems.label: B
stems.text: Tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: There is no change in attenuation with changes in tube current (changing the mA does not change the energy of the x-rays in the beam)

stems.label: C
stems.text: Slice thickness
stems.explanation: Increased slice thickness will result in more partial volume effects. The calculated CT number of the pixel is an average across the tissues contained within the voxel

stems.label: D
stems.text: Surrounding patient anatomy
stems.explanation: Beam hardening occurs when the x-rays pass through dense bone. This increases the average energy of the transmitted beam and makes it more penetrating so any other tissues the beam passes through appear to be less attenuating (the CT number decreases)

stems.label: E
stems.text: Reconstruction algorithm used
stems.explanation: The reconstruction algorithm affects the resolution and noise proerties of the CT slices, which in turn can affect the CT numbers

title: Increasing the pitch of a MDCT scan from 1.0 to 1.5 will have

stems.label: A
stems.text: Reduced image noise
stems.explanation: Increasing the pitch actually increases image noise. This is because a higher pitch acquires fewer projections, resulting in less data used to reconstruct the image and a lower signal-to-noise ratio.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Reduced patient dose
stems.explanation: For a pitch > 1 the table moves further than the beam width during one rotation, leading to a smaller volume of tissue being irradiated. This reduces the radiation dose to the patient

stems.label: C
stems.text: Reduced scan time
stems.explanation: A higher pitch allows the table to move faster, covering more anatomy in the same amount of time. This results in shorter scan times.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Reduced partial volume artifacts
stems.explanation: Z-plane resolution is degraded resulting in greater averaging between gantry rotations

stems.label: E
stems.text: Reduced patient motion artifacts
stems.explanation: A shorter duration scan means less chance of patient motion

title: Comparing reconstruction techniques in CT imaging

stems.label: A
stems.text: Filtered back projection (FBP) is generally faster at reconstructing images compared to statistical iterative reconstruction (SIR).
stems.explanation: FBP is a simpler and computationally less demanding technique, resulting in faster reconstruction times. SIR involves iterative calculations and more complex processing, which can take longer.

stems.label: B
stems.text: SIR methods are more effective at suppressing image noise, particularly in lowdose CT scans.
stems.explanation: SIR excels at noise reduction by incorporating statistical models and iterative refinement to estimate the image. This makes it particularly valuable for low-dose CT, where noise is more prominent.

stems.label: C
stems.text: FBP typically produces images with sharper edges and finer details compared to SIR.
stems.explanation: FBP often prioritizes edge enhancement and fine detail preservation, resulting in sharper images. However, this can come at the cost of increased noise. SIR may sometimes produce slightly less sharp images due to its focus on noise reduction.

stems.label: D
stems.text: FBP is better at handling artifacts caused by metal implants or beam hardening compared to SIR.
stems.explanation: SIR techniques are generally more robust in handling artifacts like metal streaks and beam hardening. They can incorporate corrections for these effects into the reconstruction process, leading to improved image quality.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Both FBP and SIR are equally susceptible to motion artifacts.
stems.explanation: Both techniques are vulnerable to motion artifacts, as patient movement during the scan can introduce blurring and distortions regardless of the reconstruction method. Minimizing patient motion is crucial for optimal image quality with either technique.

title: Decreasing each of the following parameters will reduce the

stems.label: A
stems.text: Gantry rotation speed
stems.explanation: A slower rotation speed means a longer acquisition time per rotation, which means more x-rays are detected per rotation. This will reduce statistical noise.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Slice thickness
stems.explanation: Thinner slices result in fewer photons being used per voxel, which will increase statistical (random) noise.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Tube votage (kVp)
stems.explanation: Lower kVp results in fewer X-ray photons being produced, which will increase noise.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Matrix size
stems.explanation: A smaller matrix size (going from 512x512 to 256x256) means larger pixels, hence more x-rays per voxel will be recorded and this will reduce statistical noise and increasing noise.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: Lower mA results in fewer X-ray photons being emitted each second and therefore, fewer x-rays being detected. This will increase statistical (random) noise.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Dental fillings often cause streak artifacts in CT brain scans
stems.explanation: Streak artifacts are caused by the high attenuation of X-rays by dense objects. These objects can cause inconsistencies in the projection data, leading to streaks or dark bands in the reconstructed image.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Ring artifacts appear as concentric circles in the image and are typically caused by patient motion during the scan.
stems.explanation: Ring artifacts are caused by faulty detectors in the CT scanner. If a single detector or a group of detectors malfunction, they can produce a ring-shaped artifact in the image.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Cupping artifacts between dense objects are caused by beam hardening
stems.explanation: Beam hardening occurs when lower-energy X-rays are preferentially absorbed as the beam passes through dense objects. This can lead to a non-uniform beam and result in cupping artifacts (darker areas in the centre of the image) or dark streaks between dense objects.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Zebra artifacts often occur in axial acquisitions of the head and neck
stems.explanation: Zebra artifacts are typically caused by helical interpolation algorithms used in MDCT and appear as stripes or bands in the z-direction, often near high-contrast interfaces. They won't appear in an axial CT acquisition.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Motion artifacts always appear as clearly defined streaks in the direction of motion.
stems.explanation: While motion artifacts can appear as streaks, they can also manifest as blurring, ghosting, or other distortions depending on the type and direction of the movement. The appearance of motion artifacts can be quite varied.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The frequency of electromagnetic radiation needed to excite nuclei is proportional to the static magnetic field strength
stems.explanation: The resonant frequency of the nuclei is known as the Larmor frequency. Larmor frequency is proportional to the magnetic field strength

stems.label: B
stems.text: The direction of the static magnetic field must be parallel to the long axis of the body
stems.explanation: The main magnetic field could be applied in any direction

stems.label: C
stems.text: A magnetic field gradient is used to define the slice to be imaged
stems.explanation: The magnetic field gradient causes the Larmor frequency to increase with distance along one axis. An RF pulse applied at one particular frequency will excite the nuclei in a slice of tissue where the Larmor frequency matches that of the RF pulse.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Gadolinium-based contrast agents shorten both T1 and T2 of tissues
stems.explanation: Gadolinium is a paramagnetic substance that causes both T1 & T2 to decrease. The effect on T1 is much greater than that for T2.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Hydrogen nuclei in fat and water precess at the same frequency
stems.explanation: Protons in fat & water precess at slightly different frequencies due to differences in the magnetic shielding effect of their orbital electrons

title: During the acquisition of an MR image

stems.label: A
stems.text: A slice select gradient is permanently applied along the major axis of the body
stems.explanation: The slice select gradient is only switched on when an RF pulse is applied

stems.label: B
stems.text: The slice thickness depends on the bandwidth of the RF pulse
stems.explanation: The bandwidth is the range of frequencies present in the RF pulse. A wide bandwidth will excite spins with a greater range of Larmor frequencies and so the slice thickness will also increase

stems.label: C
stems.text: A frequency encode gradient is applied while the MR signal is measured
stems.explanation: This causes the frequency of the measured signal to be dependent on position along the axis.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The spins within each slice are sequentially dephased to provide spatial information
stems.explanation: The phase encode gradient (PEG) introduces a phase change along the vertical axis of a transaxial slice. The strength (ie slope) of the gradient is increased incrementally during the acquisition of a single slice. The number of increments is equal to the matrix size, eg for a 128x128 matrix the pulse sequence needs to be repeated 128 times with a different PEG strength each time

stems.label: E
stems.text: The acquisition time is proportional to the matrix size
stems.explanation: The number of phase encode gradient increments is equal to the matrix size. So changing the matrix size will change how many times the pulse sequence must be repeated

title: In MRI, signal-to-noise ratio can be increased by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increasing the slice thickness
stems.explanation: Thicker slices will contain more nuclei, which will generate a greater signal

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing the time to echo (TE)
stems.explanation: As TE increases there will be greater decay of the signal prior to readout

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increasing the bandwidth of the receiver
stems.explanation: The receiver bandwidth is the range of frequencies detected by the receiver coil. The MR signal will contain a limited range of frequencies whereas the signal from noise has a much broader spectrum. Increasing the receiver bandwidth will result in relatively more noise being detected.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increasing the field of view
stems.explanation: As FoV increases the pixel size will also increase (the same number of pixels are sampling a larger area). Therefore, voxels get bigger and generate larger signals.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing the number of phase encoding steps
stems.explanation: This will improve spatial resolution along the phase encoding axis, but will not improve the SNR

stems.label: A
stems.text: They have three sets of gradient coils
stems.explanation: Each gradient coil is needed to obtain data in 3-dimensions

stems.label: B
stems.text: The main magnet is surrounded by cryogenic liquids
stems.explanation: Most modern scanners have “superconducting” magnets and these must be maintained at very low (ie cryogenic) temperatures for them to work properly

stems.label: C
stems.text: The RF coil can be used to detect the MR signal
stems.explanation: A single RF coil can be used to both stimulate the protons in the body (by emitting a 90o pulse) and also detecting the MR signal emitted

stems.label: D
stems.text: They must be quenched at the start of each day
stems.explanation: Quenching refers to the removal of cryogenic liquids from the magnet and will cause the main magnetic field (Bo) to vanish

stems.label: E
stems.text: They have a fringe field extending to several metres from the bore of the scanner
stems.explanation: The Bo field extends beyond the boundaries of the scanner room and can present a hazard to people in the vicinity
